n:
- *Then the LORD called to Moses and spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting:* Leviticus is part of the ongoing story of the first five books of the Bible ({{Genesis 1:1|Genesis 1:1–}}{{Deuteronomy 34:12|Deuteronomy 34:12}}). It is part of the history of God's saving actions. God chose Israel to be his people. He freed them from slavery in Egypt. Then, he made a covenant (special agreement) with them. Finally, God led them through the desert to the land promised to Abraham and his descendants. 

Leviticus continues the story in {{Exodus 40:34-38|Exodus 40:34–38}}. The Israelites had finished constructing the Tent of Meeting (the tabernacle). They consecrated the tabernacle (declared it holy) and the Lord filled it with his glory. Now, the Lord gives Moses instructions for how to worship at the tabernacle. 

- *the Tent of Meeting *(*s*ee study note on Exod 27:21): This was God's palace represented on earth. Inside the Most Holy Place, the ark of the Covenant (or Testimony) represented God's throne ({{Exodus 40:1-33|Exodus 40:1–33}}). The Lord's glory was between the cherubim's outstretched wings. This was where God would meet with the people of Israel. He would speak to them and tell them what he wanted them to do (see {{Exodus 25:22|Exodus 25:22}}).

The first part of Leviticus describes the sacrifices made by the priests in the holy tent.

These included burnt offerings, grain offerings, friendship offerings, sin offerings and guilt offerings.

The Israelites made offerings and sacrifices for different reasons. Some offerings were made simply because people wanted to make them. Others were required by God. And some were made when a priest was preparing to start serving God.

The offerings and sacrifices were made from things the people had. They could sacrifice animals that cost a lot of money like a bull. They could sacrifice smaller livestock or even birds that didn’t cost as much. They could also sacrifice bread or flour.

Everyone in the community could worship God through sacrifices and offerings. It didn’t matter how rich or poor they were. It didn’t matter if they were important leaders, priests or common people. The people were responsible for bringing their sacrifices and offerings to the holy tent. The priests were responsible for making the sacrifice and taking care of what was left.

Sacrifices were one way people showed that they obeyed, trusted and loved God. For this reason, the smell of the sacrifices pleased God. The smell also reminded God’s people that God provided the good things in their lives.

The first major section of Leviticus explains the sacrificial system and the priesthood. There were sacrifices for atonement (whole burnt offering, sin offering, and guilt offering). And there were sacrifices for worship (grain offering and peace offering). Each sacrifice taught Israel about God's character in practice. 

Priests led the sacrificial worship at the Tent of Meeting (the tabernacle). They taught the people about God's revelations to Moses at Sinai. They represented the people before God, especially on the Day of Atonement (chapter {{Leviticus 16:1-34|16}}). Priests received a portion of the offerings for their support.

- *When:* This introduces a major category, which is the process of presenting an offering. This is followed by conditions introduced by "if" ({{Leviticus 1:3|1:3}}, {{Leviticus 1:10|10}}, {{Leviticus 1:14|14}}). {{Leviticus 1:2-6:7|Leviticus 1:2–6:7}} uses this *when/if* pattern throughout all the major offerings it describes. 

- *offering* (Hebrew *qorban;* see study note on Mark 7:11) is a general term for all kinds of offerings and gifts, including those described in {{Leviticus 1:1-7:38|Leviticus 1–7}}.

*an unblemished male:* God allowed female and slightly deformed animals for some offerings not made for atonement (see {{Leviticus 3:1|3:1}}; {{Leviticus 4:27-31|4:27–31}}; {{Leviticus 22:23|22:23}}). But the people could not use them for the whole burnt offering. In the dry, brush-covered hills of southern Palestine, raising cattle was harder than raising sheep or goats. This made a bull without defects very valuable. Centuries later, the prophet Malachi confronted the people for offering sick and lame animals instead of those without defects ({{Malachi 1:6-14|Malachi 1:6–14}}).

*burnt offering* (Hebrew* ‘olah*, which means “what goes up”): The Hebrew word suggests the animal rises up in flame and smoke. Its hide was not burned, but given to the officiating priest as payment ({{Leviticus 7:8|Leviticus 7:8}}). They completely burned this offering on the altar ({{Leviticus 1:9|1:9}}). 

Its purpose was to turn away God’s judgment against sin. It also makes the worshiper clean in a ceremonial way and restores his or her relationship with God (compare {{Romans 3:25|Romans 3:25}}; {{Romans 8:3|8:3}}; {{2 Corinthians 5:18-21|2 Corinthians 5:18–21}}). The whole burnt offering appears first in this list of offerings ({{Leviticus 1:1-7:38|Leviticus 1–7}}). It sets a pattern for the offerings that follow. It is the most common offering for atonement.

- *He is to lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering:* The sacrificial animal represented the worshiper in the ceremony ({{Leviticus 4:4|Leviticus 4:4}}, {{Leviticus 4:15|15}}, {{Leviticus 4:24|24}}, {{Leviticus 4:29|29}}, {{Leviticus 4:33|33}}; {{Leviticus 16:21|16:21}}). This act showed that the animal's death represented the owner's death. During the Day of Atonement ceremony, it showed that God transferred the owner's sins to the animal ({{Leviticus 16:20-22|16:20–22}}). In the peace offering ({{Leviticus 3:2|3:2}}, {{Leviticus 3:8|8}}, {{Leviticus 3:13|13}}), the act probably showed ownership of the sacrificed animal. 

- The phrase *on his behalf* may mean “as payment for sin” (sometimes called *expiation*) or “as a substitute for the sinner’s death” (sometimes called *propitiation*). 

- *to make atonement for him:* While older commentaries describe this as “covering over” sin, recent studies define it as “blotting out, erasing, or cleansing from” sin. The concept involves turning away God’s judgment against sin, making the worshiper clean in a ceremonial way, and restoring fellowship with God and with the community of God’s people.

- *Aaron’s sons:* Moses was from the tribe of Levi. This tribe divided into two groups: 

- priests, who were descendants of Aaron, the first high priest; and 

- Levites, who served in supporting roles ({{Exodus 28:1-4|Exodus 28:1–4}}; {{Numbers 18:1-7|Numbers 18:1–7}}). 

These instructions also applied to future generations. 

- *the blood: *This symbolized life, not death. The basis of the Israelite sacrifice system was substitution. Shedding sacrificial blood was essential for atonement. It meant sacrificing the animal's life as a substitute for the worshiper's life ({{Leviticus 17:10-14|Leviticus 17:10–14}}; {{Hebrews 9:22|Hebrews 9:22}}). Jesus Christ's shed his blood as the ultimate sacrifice for sin ({{Hebrews 9:11-14|Hebrews 9:11–14}}). 

- *the altar* of burnt offering was at the east end of the courtyard. It was outside the Tent of Meeting but inside the courtyard entrance ({{Exodus 40:6|Exodus 40:6}}, {{Exodus 40:29|29}}).
The priest would burn the whole animal, except for the skin, which he kept as his share of the offering ({{Leviticus 7:8|Leviticus 7:8}}).

The Hebrew word for *fat* refers to the suet, or hard fat, around the kidneys and loins. This term appears only here and in {{Leviticus 1:12|Leviticus 1:12}} and {{Leviticus 8:20|8:20}}. All fat (not just this specific fat) belonged to God ({{Leviticus 3:14-17|3:14–17}}; {{Leviticus 7:23-25|7:23–25}}; see {{1 Samuel 2:15-17|1 Samuel 2:15–17}}). The whole burnt offering was the only offering completely burned on the altar. For other offerings, they burned the fatty parts and some internal organs. The rest belonged to the officiating priests and sometimes the worshiper ({{Leviticus 7:11-18|Leviticus 7:11–18}}).

- They washed the offering with water to remove dirt or debris that might contaminate it. Washing was also necessary for purification from ceremonial uncleanness, a requirement for serving in the Tent of Meeting ({{Leviticus 6:27|Leviticus 6:27}}; {{Leviticus 11:28|11:28}}). 

- *an offering made by fire:* Traditional Bible versions translate the Hebrew term *’isheh* this way. Although they did burn the offering ({{Leviticus 1:13|Leviticus 1:13}}, {{Leviticus 1:17|17}}), recent research suggests the word meant “gift.” 

- *a pleasing aroma to the LORD *(literally *a restful odor;* also in {{Leviticus 1:13|Leviticus 1:13}}, {{Leviticus 1:17|17}}): Pagans in the ancient Near East believed their gods smelled the offerings because they needed to eat them to live. God's response is sometimes described in ways that reflect this cultural setting (for example, {{Leviticus 21:6|Leviticus 21:6}}; {{Numbers 28:2|Numbers 28:2}}). Yet, the Bible makes it clear that God did not need offerings as food ({{Psalm 50:9-13|Psalm 50:9–13}}). Instead, they pleased him as sincere offerings for atonement.

The law allowed poorer Israelites to offer smaller animals so that atonement (a sacrifice that removes guilt and restores fellowship with God) would be more affordable. The way these animals were offered was very similar to the way bulls were offered ({{Leviticus 1:3-9|Leviticus 1:3–9}}).

Birds were plentiful, cheap, and easy to catch. This allowed both rich and poor people to participate in sacrifices for atonement and worship (see also {{Leviticus 5:7|Leviticus 5:7}}; {{Leviticus 12:8|12:8}}; see {{Luke 2:24|Luke 2:24}}).

*tear … without dividing the bird completely: *Cutting larger animals into pieces (like {{Leviticus 1:6|Leviticus 1:6}}, {{Leviticus 1:12|12}}) probably reflects an ancient covenant-making ceremony. In this ceremony, participants passed between the two halves of a sacrificed animal (see {{Genesis 15:10|Genesis 15:10}}). Because of their small size, people did not cut birds in half. If passing between them was necessary, they arranged the birds in pairs.

- *fine flour *was choice wheat flour, unlike common barley flour. See also {{1 Kings 4:22|1 Kings 4:22}}; {{Ezekiel 16:13|Ezekiel 16:13}}, {{Ezekiel 16:19|19}}. 

- Israelites used *olive oil *for cooking, as lamp fuel, and for medicine and cosmetics. It represented the land's rich produce and God's provision ({{Deuteronomy 8:8|Deuteronomy 8:8}}). 

- Like *fine flour*, Scripture often links *frankincense *with the tabernacle ({{Exodus 30:34|Exodus 30:34}}; {{Leviticus 24:7|Leviticus 24:7}}) or the temple ({{1 Chronicles 9:29|1 Chronicles 9:29}}). Individuals also used this fragrant tree resin on special occasions ({{Song of Songs 3:6|Song of Solomon 3:6}}; {{Matthew 2:11|Matthew 2:11}}). It was a main ingredient in the holy incense burned in the Holy Place as a physical expression of worship ({{Exodus 30:34-38|Exodus 30:34–38}}).

The* grain offering* (Hebrew *minkhah*, meaning “gift” or “present”) allowed people to worship the Lord by giving a gift. It acknowledged the Lord's authority over the worshiper's life. People gave the grain offering with each whole burnt offering ({{Numbers 28:3-6|Numbers 28:3–6}}, {{Numbers 28:12-13|12–13}}), sin offering ({{Numbers 6:14-15|Numbers 6:14–15}}), and peace offering ({{Leviticus 9:4|Leviticus 9:4}}; {{Numbers 6:17|Numbers 6:17}}). The grain offering provided bread for the priest's daily needs, as priests did not have farmland.
The priest burned the main part of the grain offering on the altar. This reminded the worshiper that the whole offering belonged to God.

- *The remainder of the grain offering:* They usually reserved a part of the fire offerings for the priest as food (see {{Leviticus 6:16-17|6:16–17}}). Exceptions included:

- the whole burnt offering, where the priest only received the hide (see {{Leviticus 7:8|7:8}}),

- offerings given by the priest for himself ({{Leviticus 4:3-12|4:3–12}}; {{Leviticus 6:19-23|6:19–23}}), or

- offerings made for the entire community ({{Leviticus 4:13-21|4:13–21}}). 

In these cases, they completely burned the offering. The grain offering provided the priests with bread for their diet. 

- *most holy part* (Hebrew *qodesh qodashim*, which means “holy of holies”): Both God and what belongs to God are holy. The *most holy part *refers to the priestly share taken from the holy offering and reserved for a special purpose. {{Numbers 18:8-10|Numbers 18:8–10}}uses this term for the priest’s share of any gifts dedicated to the Lord.

- They placed a large ceramic oven in a hole and lit a fire around it. Once the oven was hot, they baked flat cakes or wafers against its inner wall. 

- *unleavened:* See study note on 2:11; see also {{Exodus 12:8|Exodus 12:8}}.
A *griddle* was a flat stone or clay surface placed over a fire to heat it. Later, people made griddles from metal ({{Ezekiel 4:3|Ezekiel 4:3}}).
The people fried dough in a pan with oil until it was crisp.

- *leaven:* The bread eaten in biblical times was like modern sourdough. What is often called *leaven* was wild yeast spores mixed into moist dough or flour. The leaven would grow, fermenting and becoming sour and raising the dough. They would save a portion of this sour dough to knead into future batches ({{Matthew 13:33|Matthew 13:33}}). 

Unleavened bread was necessary for Passover ({{Exodus 12:8|Exodus 12:8}}). This was to remember Israel's slavery in Egypt ({{Deuteronomy 16:3|Deuteronomy 16:3}}) and their quick departure ({{Exodus 12:34|Exodus 12:34}}; {{Exodus 13:3|13:3}}). After the exodus, unleavened bread became altar bread. They could not burn leavened bread on the altar. 

- *honey: *The Hebrew word *debash* may also mean "fruit nectar." It is unknown why they did not burn it. But it might relate to its use in pagan offerings, especially to underworld gods. If it means "fruit nectar," its link with wine and fermentation might have connected it with leaven, making it unsuitable for the altar. 

Yet, they could use both honey and yeast in first crop offerings ({{Leviticus 2:12|Leviticus 2:12}}). They would present loaves made with leaven with thank offerings ({{Leviticus 7:13|7:13}}). They gave them to the priest during the Festival of Harvest ({{Leviticus 23:17|23:17}}). 

In the New Testament, leaven becomes a spiritual symbol, highlighting its sour taste and how it spreads ({{Matthew 16:6|Matthew 16:6}}, {{Matthew 16:11|11}}, {{Matthew 16:12|12}}; {{1 Corinthians 5:6-8|1 Corinthians 5:6–8}}; see also {{Matthew 13:33|Matthew 13:33}}).

*as an offering of firstfruits: *Offering the first crops involved giving the first part of the harvest ({{Leviticus 23:15-21|Leviticus 23:15–21}}; {{Numbers 28:26-31|Numbers 28:26–31}}). Like the main portion of the grain offering, this act acknowledged that the entire harvest belonged to God ({{Leviticus 23:10-11|Leviticus 23:10–11}}; {{Exodus 22:29|Exodus 22:29}}; {{Exodus 23:19|23:19}}; {{Exodus 34:26|34:26}}; {{Numbers 15:18-20|Numbers 15:18–20}}; {{Deuteronomy 18:4-5|Deuteronomy 18:4–5}}; {{Deuteronomy 26:1-2|26:1–2}}). It also recognized that the land itself, not just its produce, belonged to God. Israel was only the tenant (see {{Leviticus 25:23|Leviticus 25:23}}).

In ancient times, people considered salt as a symbol of what is permanent because salt preserved food. *The salt of the covenant* represented a lasting agreement renewed with each new generation (see study notes on Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 13:5).

- *male or female: *The whole burnt offering required male animals because it made atonement ({{Leviticus 1:3|Leviticus 1:3}}, {{Leviticus 1:10|10}}). The less formal peace offering allowed both male and female animals (see also {{Leviticus 4:28|4:28}}, {{Leviticus 4:32|32}}). 

- *without blemish:* The sacrificial animals had to be healthy. The only exception was the voluntary offering, which allowed a slight blemish ({{Leviticus 22:23|22:23}}).

The *peace offering* (called *shelem* in Hebrew) showed worship through fellowship with the Lord and others. The word comes from the same root as *shalom,* which means wholeness, well-being, harmony, and peace. 

*Shalom* is more than just ending conflict between God and the worshiper. It means a bond of harmonious fellowship. The peace offering was a shared meal celebrating fellowship with God and others (compare {{Exodus 18:12|Exodus 18:12}}; {{Exodus 24:9-11|24:9–11}}; {{1 Samuel 9:15-24|1 Samuel 9:15–24}}). They could offer it as thanks ({{Leviticus 7:12-15|Leviticus 7:12–15}}), as a voluntary offering, or to fulfill a vow ({{Leviticus 7:16-18|7:16–18}}; {{Leviticus 22:21|22:21}}). 

Peace offerings often came after whole burnt offerings (for example, {{1 Kings 9:25|1 Kings 9:25}}). This showed that fellowship with God follows atonement. When we experience atonement through Christ, we can be at peace with God and each other (see {{Acts 2:42|Acts 2:42}}; {{Acts 10:36|10:36}}; {{Romans 5:1|Romans 5:1}}; {{1 Corinthians 10:16|1 Corinthians 10:16}}; {{1 Corinthians 11:17-34|11:17–34}}; {{2 Corinthians 5:18-21|2 Corinthians 5:18–21}}).

*kidneys … lobe of the liver*: The kidneys and liver had special meaning for the Israelites. 

They thought of kidneys as the place where understanding and deep thoughts came from, similar to how we think of the brain today. For example, "my heart yearns within me" [literally *my kidneys are consumed*] ({{Job 19:27|Job 19:27}}). It can refer to "minds" ({{Psalm 7:9|Psalms 7:9}}; {{Psalm 26:2|Psalm 26:2}}; {{Jeremiah 17:10|Jeremiah 17:10}}; {{Jeremiah 11:20|Jeremiah 11:20}}; {{Jeremiah 20:12|20:12}}). 

The liver represented life and energy to the Israelites, similar to how many cultures today understand the "heart" ({{Lamentations 2:11|Lamentations 2:11}}).

{{Leviticus 1:3-17|Leviticus 1:3–17}} describes the burnt offering. It is more accurate to call it "the whole burnt offering." They offered it twice daily (see {{Numbers 28:4|Numbers 28:4}}). God required atonement before fellowship with him. So, the text assumes the burnt offering was already on the altar. The priest would place the fatty portions and certain internal organs of the peace offering on top of it ({{Leviticus 3:3-4|Leviticus 3:3–4}}).
Sheep were smaller, easier to raise, and less expensive than cattle. Besides the exceptions mentioned in these verses, people offered sheep as sacrifices in the same way as cattle.
*fat tail:* In this region of the ancient Near East, sheep had wide, fatty tails. People burned these tails on the altar with the other fat.

- *an offering made by fire:* See study note on Leviticus 1:9. 

- The Scripture calls offerings of food “the food of … God” ({{Leviticus 21:6|Leviticus 21:6}}, {{Leviticus 21:8|8}}, {{Leviticus 21:17|17}}, {{Leviticus 21:21|21}}, {{Leviticus 21:22|22}}; {{Numbers 28:2|Numbers 28:2}}). Yet, Scripture clearly states that the Lord did not eat the offerings, unlike pagan beliefs about their gods ({{Psalm 50:9-13|Psalm 50:9–13}}). Instead, these offerings belonged to God, and the priest ate a portion as God’s representative ({{Leviticus 21:21-22|Leviticus 21:21–22}}). These offerings provided for the priest and his family.
The offering of goats followed a similar pattern to that of cattle and sheep. People considered both goats and sheep as offerings from the flock (see {{Leviticus 3:6|Leviticus 3:6}}).
God did not allow the people to eat *any fat or any blood* (see {{Leviticus 1:5|Leviticus 1:5}}, {{Leviticus 1:8|8}}, and study notes).

The sin offering is called* khatta’t *in Hebrew, from the root *khata’.* It means "to lack, fall short, miss, fail." The people made this offering when they unintentionally violated specific commands of God (see also {{Numbers 15:22-29|Numbers 15:22–29}}). The purpose of this offering was to repair a loss or fix a failure (for example, {{Leviticus 5:1-4|Leviticus 5:1–4}}). 

Although all Christians sin, God will forgive us if we confess them ({{Galatians 6:1|Galatians 6:1}}; {{1 John 1:8-9|1 John 1:8–9}}). Yet, the Scripture warns against sinning "defiantly" or "deliberately" {{Hebrews 6:4-6|(}}{{Numbers 15:30-31|Numbers 15:30–31}}; {{Hebrews 10:26-29|Hebrews 10:26–29}}; {{Hebrews 6:4-6|6:4–6}}).

- God chose the high priest for a special role and they *anointed* him. The Hebrew word for "anoint" is *mashiakh. *It means "set apart by the ritual of anointing." In {{1 Samuel 1:1|1 Samuel 1:1—2 Kings 25:30}}, anointing usually refers to Israel's king (see {{1 Samuel 24:6|1 Samuel 24:6}}; {{2 Samuel 1:14|2 Samuel 1:14}}; {{2 Samuel 19:21|19:21}}). 

They would anoint all priests ({{Exodus 40:13-15|Exodus 40:13–15}}). Yet, here the term probably refers to the high priest because they specially anointed him for service in the tabernacle ({{Leviticus 6:20|Leviticus 6:20}}; {{Leviticus 8:12|8:12}}). The high priest acted as a mediator or intercessor for all of Israel, including other priests. His sin would bring guilt on the entire community (see “Community Identity” Theme Note). 

- Guilt in this sense comes from disobeying God’s will. It is not only a feeling in the mind but a real offense against God (see study note on Leviticus 5:17–19).

These verses describe two types of sin offerings: 

- The offering for the sin of the high priest ({{Leviticus 4:3|Leviticus 4:3}}, {{Leviticus 4:20|20}}) and the entire Israelite community ({{Leviticus 4:13|4:13}}).

- The offering for one of Israel’s leaders ({{Leviticus 4:22|4:22}}) and any common person ({{Leviticus 4:27|4:27}}). 

The first type required a bull, a large and expensive animal. It was not eaten ({{Leviticus 6:30|6:30}}) but completely burned ({{Leviticus 4:12|4:12}}, {{Leviticus 4:21|21}}). The priests presented some of its blood in the Holy Place ({{Leviticus 4:6-7|4:6–7}}, {{Leviticus 4:17-18|17–18}}). 

The second type required a smaller animal. This was a male goat for a leader or a female sheep or goat for a common person. The priest ate part of the common person’s offering ({{Leviticus 6:24-29|6:24–29}}). The priest would present the blood at the bronze altar in the courtyard ({{Leviticus 4:25|4:25}}, {{Leviticus 4:30|30}}). 

This distinction highlights the responsibilities of leaders. The offering was the same for the priest and the entire community. But the leader’s offering was more than that of a common person. 

The New Testament also emphasizes the responsibility of religious leaders. God will judge those who teach and those who serve as religious leaders more strictly than their followers ({{James 3:1|James 3:1}}; {{Matthew 23:1-33|Matthew 23:1–33}}; {{Luke 20:47|Luke 20:47}}).

The tabernacle area had a tent (sometimes called the “Tent of Meeting”; (see study note on 1:1). The tent was at the west end of the courtyard. Inside the tent, an inner curtain separated the first room, the Holy Place, from the second, the Most Holy Place. The Most Holy Place contained the ark of the Covenant (or Testimony) and represented God's throne room ({{Exodus 26:31-33|Exodus 26:31–33}}; see study note on Leviticus 1:1). 

The priests would sprinkle the animal's blood in front of the curtain ({{Leviticus 4:6|Leviticus 4:6}}, {{Leviticus 4:17|17}}). They would also apply it to the horns of the incense altar ({{Leviticus 4:7|4:7}}, {{Leviticus 4:18|18}}). This would atone for the anointed priest or the entire congregation. This action showed the seriousness of the offenses that needed atonement (compare {{Leviticus 4:25|4:25}}, {{Leviticus 4:30-35|30–35}}).

*the altar for fragrant incense: *This was in front of the inner curtain, just outside the Most Holy Place ({{Leviticus 4:6|Leviticus 4:6}}). It had four projections that looked like horns, similar to the altar for burnt offerings (see study note on Exodus 27:2). The priests burned incense on this altar to the Lord each morning and evening ({{Exodus 30:1-10|Exodus 30:1–10}}).

They would only burn the offerings for the priest or the entire community outside the camp. God might have commanded this because the offering had symbolically taken on the impurity (uncleanness) of the high priest or the community. So, they had to remove it outside the camp. The guilty people could not participate in or gain any benefit from their own sin offerings. This was true even for priests ({{Leviticus 6:19-23|Leviticus 6:19–23}}).

The Hebrew word for *elders* is related to the word for "beard." It suggests maturity but not necessarily old age. Elders were community leaders, usually leaders of families and tribes (see {{Exodus 18:21-26|Exodus 18:21–26}}; {{Deuteronomy 22:15-19|Deuteronomy 22:15–19}}). For this offering, the elders represented all the people, as they did later when anointing David as king ({{2 Samuel 5:3|2 Samuel 5:3}}).

The phrase *they will be forgiven* often appears in passages about atonement ({{Leviticus 4:26|Leviticus 4:26}}, {{Leviticus 4:31|31}}, {{Leviticus 4:35|35}}; {{Leviticus 5:10|5:10}}, {{Leviticus 5:13|13}}, {{Leviticus 5:16|16}}, {{Leviticus 5:18|18}}; {{Leviticus 6:7|6:7}}; {{Leviticus 19:22|19:22}}; {{Numbers 15:25|Numbers 15:25}}, {{Numbers 15:26|26}}, {{Numbers 15:28|28}}). God is willing to forgive a repentant person's sin and allow him or her to return to the community of faith.
Israel's leaders included the elders (see {{Leviticus 4:15|Leviticus 4:15}}), chiefs of tribes and families (see {{Numbers 1:16|Numbers 1:16}}, {{Numbers 1:44|44}}; {{1 Kings 8:1|1 Kings 8:1}}).

The sin offerings in this passage atoned for the common people, including leaders and other Israelites. These offerings could be eaten, unlike those in {{Leviticus 4:3-21|Leviticus 4:3–21}}, and involved smaller animals. They disposed of the blood in the tabernacle courtyard, not the Holy Place. 

Like the peace offering in chapter {{Leviticus 3:1-17|3}}, they burned the fat and certain internal organs on the altar. The priest and his male family members ate the rest of the meat in a holy place ({{Leviticus 6:29|6:29}}; {{Leviticus 6:26|6:26}}; compare {{Leviticus 10:16-20|10:16–20}}). A lay leader offered a male goat ({{Leviticus 4:23|4:23}}), while a common person could offer a female goat or lamb. 

The smaller size and cost of the animal reflected that the common person had less influence. It probably related to their financial situation as well. Those who were poor could bring a pair of doves or young pigeons ({{Leviticus 5:7-8|5:7–8}}; {{Leviticus 12:6|12:6}}, {{Leviticus 12:8|8}}; compare {{Luke 2:24|Luke 2:24}}). The very poor could offer two quarts of flour ({{Leviticus 5:11|Leviticus 5:11}}).

The* male goat *offered by a leader from the common people was less than the priest's required offering. A priest must offer a bull. But the leader must offer more than a common person's requirement (see {{Leviticus 4:28|Leviticus 4:28}}, {{Leviticus 4:32|32}}). Yet, like all offerings for atonement, the animal could not have any defects (see {{Leviticus 1:3|1:3}}).
*at the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered:* See {{Leviticus 1:3-5|Leviticus 1:3–5}}.

*blood … horns of the altar:* They did not take the blood of a leader's offering ({{Leviticus 4:25|Leviticus 4:25}}) or a common Israelite's offering ({{Leviticus 4:30|4:30}}, {{Leviticus 4:34|34}}) into the Holy Place. The blood of the priest's bull offering entered the Holy Place. The priest who offered would eat a portion of the meat ({{Leviticus 6:24-29|6:24–29}}).

The common people, with fewer responsibilities than priests or leaders, could offer a female sheep or goat. More important social positions required more responsibility (see {{Amos 3:2|Amos 3:2}}; {{Matthew 25:14-30|Matthew 25:14–30}}; {{James 3:1|James 3:1}}).

- The first sin was not testifying when summoned as a witness in court. This verse considers not testifying to be an active sin. This was because it helped the criminal. 

- *he shall bear the iniquity:* Expecting God's punishment for the sin, the guilty person offered a sacrifice to remove the guilt and escape the punishment.

These verses give examples of sins that required a sin offering ({{Leviticus 4:2|Leviticus 4:2}}). When a person became aware of committing a wrong, the next step to make it right was to admit the guilt and bring a sin offering.

*unclean:* "Clean" and "unclean" did not relate to hygiene (see {{Leviticus 11:1-15:33|Leviticus 11:1–15:33}}). They referred to whether someone could participate in worship. For animals, it meant if they were suitable for sacrifice or eating. There is a list of ceremonially clean and unclean animals in {{Leviticus 11:1-47|11:1–47}}. 

To become ceremonially clean after touching an unclean animal, a person had to wash their clothes. They also had to stay away from the community until evening ({{Leviticus 11:25|11:25}}). This sin offering probably shows that the person did not follow the rules for cleansing ({{Leviticus 11:27-28|11:27–28}}).

Any bodily discharge, including blood, made a person temporarily unclean (chapters {{Leviticus 11:1-15:33|Leviticus 11–15}}). Being ceremonially unclean was not the same as sin. But if someone ignored their unclean state and did not take the required steps, that became sin because it allowed the impurity to spread. Once a person realized they were unclean, they were guilty if they ignored it.

People were allowed to take oaths in the name of the Lord. But making a foolish or careless vow misused the Lord’s name and showed disrespect ({{Exodus 20:7|Exodus 20:7}}). For this reason, the law required people to keep the vows they made (see {{Numbers 30:2|Numbers 30:2}}; {{Deuteronomy 23:21-23|Deuteronomy 23:21–23}}; {{Ecclesiastes 5:4-6|Ecclesiastes 5:4–6}}).

- *If someone incurs guilt:* Situations needing a sin offering assumed there was guilt that happened by accident or ignorance. Once someone realized they did something wrong, they became guilty and needed to receive atonement. If someone knew they sinned, they must deal with it. To know what was right and not do it was also a sin (see {{Leviticus 5:17|5:17}}; {{James 4:17|James 4:17}}). 

- *confess:* Offering a sacrifice for sin without admitting guilt was a pointless ceremony. When presenting the sacrificial animal to the priest, the worshiper probably explained the reason for the offering.

- The required sacrifice fulfilled the penalty (see study note on Leviticus 4:1–5:13). 

- The actions described in {{Leviticus 5:1-5|Leviticus 5:1–5}} seem to apply to orindary people, not priests. For this reason, the law allowed the use of a female animal for the offering, following the same principle shown in {{Leviticus 4:28|4:28}}, {{Leviticus 4:32|32}}.

*a sin offering: *This included part as a burnt offering and part given to the priests after they made the offering (compare {{Leviticus 4:22-35|Leviticus 4:22–35}}; {{Leviticus 6:24-30|6:24–30}}). Due to their small size, it required two birds (one for each type of offering).

Poor people also needed to receive atonement and be restored to God. For those who could not afford a lamb, the law allowed them to bring birds instead ({{Leviticus 5:7|Leviticus 5:7}}; compare {{Leviticus 1:14-17|1:14–17}}). Normally, atonement required the blood of an animal ({{Leviticus 17:11|17:11}}). But in his grace, God permitted even an offering of flour when a person was too poor to afford two birds ({{Leviticus 5:11|5:11}}).

The sin offering was not to include* olive oil or frankincense on it*. These were necessary for the grain offering, which was a person's gift to the Lord to show worship (see {{Leviticus 2:1|Leviticus 2:1}}). The sin offering, however, was different. It was meant to make atonement and bring forgiveness, so it had to be offered without anything added.

- *will make atonement for him:* See study notes on Leviticus 1:4 and 4:20. 

- *The remainder: *See study note on 2:3.

The *guilt offering* (called *’asham* in Hebrew, meaning “guilt”) dealt with cases of property loss or damage. This could be either holy property set apart for God ({{Leviticus 5:14-16|Leviticus 5:14–16}}) or ordinary property belong to a person ({{Leviticus 6:1-7|6:1–7}}). The offering required both replacement and repayment for the loss ({{Leviticus 5:16|5:16}}; {{Leviticus 6:5|6:5}}). 

This offering could be called a “penalty offering” because the ram served as a penalty. It could also be called a “replacement offering” because a person had to replace the loss before offering the ram. In the guilt offering, the loss was not only a failure in God's eyes, as with the sin offering ({{Leviticus 5:14-6:7|5:14–6:7}}). It was also a loss of property to another person or to the sanctuary. Compare {{Matthew 5:23-24|Matthew 5:23–24}}.

- *sins unintentionally: *Damage to sacred property (objects or land set apart for God) was treated differently from damage to ordinary property. A sacrifice could only restore sacred property if the damage was done by accident. If someone harmed sacred things on purpose, such as vandalizing them, it was considered blasphemy (disrespect toward God).

As with other deliberate sins, there was no specific way to atone for it (see {{Numbers 15:30-31|Numbers 15:30–31}}). A true believer would not defiantly continue in sin (see {{1 John 3:9|1 John 3:9}}). 

- *sanctuary shekel:* This was not a coin but a standardized unit of weight. They used it to evaluate the offered ram. Some scholars suggest this text allows substituting the appropriate amount of silver for the ram.

The law required an extra payment of 20 percent to make up for loss or damage to property. If the property was sacred (set apart for God), the extra payment went directly to the priests. Accidental damage to sacred property happened when someone unintentionally ate the sacred offerings or forgot the tithe ({{Leviticus 22:14|Leviticus 22:14}}; {{Leviticus 27:31|27:31}}). A similar additional charge applied when redeeming an animal ({{Leviticus 27:13|27:13}}, {{Leviticus 27:27|27}}).

This paragraph explains the main principles of the guilt offering. Even if someone did not know they did something wrong, they were still guilty and had to give the right guilt offering. This rule applied to both sacred property (set apart for God) and ordinary property ({{Leviticus 5:14-16|Leviticus 5:14–16}}; {{Leviticus 6:1-7|6:1–7}}).

*If someone sins and acts unfaithfully against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor: *FWhen a person sins against an associate, they are also unfaithful to the Lord. For believers, there is no such thing as a nonreligious (secular) sin. Every sin involves God, even when it is directed against another person or group. 

In these cases, a guilt offering was required. God’s forgiveness was needed, but the sinner first had to make restitution (pay back or repair the wrong) to the injured person ({{Leviticus 6:5-7|Leviticus 6:5–7}}; compare {{Matthew 5:23-24|Matthew 5:23–24}}). Unlike offenses against sacred property ({{Leviticus 5:14-16|Leviticus 5:14–16}}), both accidental and intentional offenses against another person’s property could be forgiven.

The instructions for the guilt offering assumed a person's conscience would lead them to voluntary repayment. When replacement was voluntary, the extra charge for loss of use to the owner was always 20 percent. Penalties were more severe in other cases (compare {{Exodus 22:1-15|Exodus 22:1–15}}). There is a clear difference between voluntary confession and admitting sin only after being caught.

*In this way the priest will make atonement for him before the LORD:* God kindly provided his people a way to atone for their sins (atonement refers to the process by which God and humanity are reconnected and brought into a personal relationship). See also study notes on 1:4; 4:20.

The regulations in {{Leviticus 1:2-6:7|Leviticus 1:2–6:7}} include instructions for both priests and ordinary Israelites. This section details the rights and duties of the priest who led the offerings. The tribe of Levi received no land for farming ({{Deuteronomy 18:1|Deuteronomy 18:1}}; {{Joshua 13:14|Joshua 13:14}}, {{Joshua 13:33|33}}). Priests relied on offerings for their income. These rules made sure the priests were properly provided for. Like many human systems, the offering system was later abused ({{1 Samuel 2:12-25|1 Samuel 2:12–25}}; {{Hosea 4:8|Hosea 4:8}}).

- The priest had to wear official linen clothing while serving at the tabernacle. This showed everyone he was performing his duties ({{Exodus 28:40-43|Exodus 28:40–43}}). The priest needed to dress properly to serve the divine king. He could not wear his official clothing outside the tabernacle ({{Leviticus 6:11|Leviticus 6:11}}; {{Ezekiel 44:19|Ezekiel 44:19}}). 

- *undergarments:* See {{Exodus 20:26|Exodus 20:26}}.
The Israelites viewed most natural places as ceremonially clean.

This passage warns that the fire on the bronze altar must always remain tended and never allowed to go out. This may anticipate the tragedy of the "unauthorized fire" offered by Nadab and Abihu ({{Leviticus 10:1-2|Leviticus 10:1–2}}).
Here, *holy place* does not refer to the Holy Place at the center of the tabernacle. It refers to any area within the tabernacle area, all of which were ceremonially clean and holy.

- *leaven:* See study note on 2:11. 

- The priests received a portion of the grain offering. This provided bread, which was their main food ({{Leviticus 7:9|7:9}}). It also had spiritual meaning, because it was considered *most holy*. See study note on 2:3.

- The priestly share was not only for the priest performing the sacrifice. All of Aaron’s male descendants shared it. The text does not explain why only males could eat these offerings, although other offerings were for all priestly family members (see study note on Leviticus 10:13–15; see also {{Numbers 18:20-24|Numbers 18:20–24}}). 

- *will become holy* (Or *must be holy;* also in {{Leviticus 6:27|Leviticus 6:27}}): Although uncleanness could spread by touch (chapter {{Leviticus 15:1-33|15}}), the prophet Haggai suggested that holiness could not ({{Haggai 2:12|Haggai 2:12}}). If a ceremonially unclean person touched something holy, it could lead to disaster ({{Leviticus 10:1-3|Leviticus 10:1–3}}; {{1 Samuel 6:19-20|1 Samuel 6:19–20}}; {{2 Samuel 6:6-8|2 Samuel 6:6–8}}).
These instructions only apply to the grain part of the ordination offering (see {{Leviticus 2:1-16|Leviticus 2:1–16}}). For the rest of the ordination offering, see {{Leviticus 8:22-32|8:22–32}}.
Only the high priest could represent the whole priesthood, including all the other priests.

Normally, most of a grain offering went to the priest who led the ceremony ({{Leviticus 2:9-10|Leviticus 2:9–10}}). But the grain offering in {{Leviticus 6:19-23|6:19–23}} was for a special event, the ordination of the priests. Ordination means setting apart the priests for their service to the Lord. This offering had to be burned completely and not eaten.

A clay pot was porous and could not be cleaned well. Some of the holy food might stick to it or soak into it. Using the pot again would dishonor what was holy.

But a bronze pot could be scrubbed clean to prevent this problem (see also {{Leviticus 11:33|Leviticus 11:33}}; {{Leviticus 15:12|15:12}}).

The anointed priest and the entire congregation could not eat some sin offerings. The priest took the blood from these offerings into the Holy Place and sprinkled it in front of the curtain (see {{Leviticus 4:1-21|Leviticus 4:1–21}}). The lay leader and the ordinary Israelites could eat the sacrifices. The priest poured the blood of these animals on and around the base of the altar in the tabernacle courtyard (see {{Leviticus 4:22-35|4:22–35}}).

- The guilt offering required sacrificing a ram ({{Leviticus 5:18|Leviticus 5:18}}). 

- *the fat … fat tail … organs:* They burned these parts of the guilt offering, just like in the peace offering ({{Leviticus 3:3-4|3:3–4}}, {{Leviticus 3:9-10|9–10}}, {{Leviticus 3:14-15|14–15}}) and the sin offering ({{Leviticus 4:8-9|4:8–9}}, {{Leviticus 4:26|26}}, {{Leviticus 4:31|31}}, {{Leviticus 4:35|35}}).

Worshipers would present the peace offering for three reasons: 

- as thanks to God, 

- as payment of a vow ({{Leviticus 7:16|Leviticus 7:16}}), or 

- as a voluntary gift (see {{Leviticus 3:1-7|3:1–7}}). 

A worshiper showed thanks by giving a grain offering with the peace offering ({{Leviticus 2:1-16|2:1–16}}). A grain offering included unleavened cakes, wafers, or fine flour cakes. They mixed all of them or spread olive oil on them. They set aside a portion to burn ({{Leviticus 2:9|2:9}}). The grain offering came with loaves of "leavened bread" ({{Leviticus 7:13|7:13}}).

Worshipers presented the thanksgiving offering as an expression of gratitude ({{Jeremiah 17:26|Jeremiah 17:26}}; {{Jeremiah 33:11|33:11}}). They had to eat the sacrifice on the same day they offered it. This rule helped the worshiper remember the reason for giving thanks.

Worshipers presented the "peace offering of thanksgiving" to show gratitude to the Lord ({{Leviticus 7:12-15|Leviticus 7:12–15}}). This was unlike the vow offering linked to a promise made by a worshiper. After, they celebrated with a meal. The meal was less formal and could continue into the next day. But since the vow offering involved a promise to God, it had stricter rules than the voluntary offering, which could even use a deformed animal ({{Leviticus 22:23|22:23}}).

The Hebrew word *piggul* means “contaminated.” It appears only three other times in the Bible ({{Leviticus 19:7|Leviticus 19:7}}; {{Isaiah 65:4|Isaiah 65:4}}; {{Ezekiel 4:14|Ezekiel 4:14}}). This term always refers to meat that is not suitable for humans to sacrifice or eat.

Anything ceremonially unclean could not touch what was holy ({{Leviticus 7:20|Leviticus 7:20}}). Although uncleanness was not sinful by itself, it symbolized what was unholy (see {{Exodus 19:10|Exodus 19:10}}).

*cut off: *This expression can mean three serious things: 

- God judged the person, and they died early from natural causes ({{Leviticus 17:10-14|Leviticus 17:10–14}}). 

- The community executed the person (see {{Exodus 31:14|Exodus 31:14}}). 

- The person lost membership in Israel. This was either by expulsion (like excommunication) or being shunned and treated as ceremonially unclean ({{Leviticus 18:24-30|Leviticus 18:24–30}}; see {{Leviticus 23:29-30|23:29–30}}, where "cut off" seems different from "destroy").

In the sacrificial system, the fat and blood of all altar offerings belonged to God. People offered them before eating any part of the sacrifice. God forbid the Israelites of consuming blood because it represented the animal's life ({{Leviticus 17:10-16|Leviticus 17:10–16}}). The rule against eating fat might have been because fat, considered the best part, belonged to God.

Animals found dead had not been drained of their blood and were therefore unclean. Their fat was unfit to offer to the Lord and the Israelites could not eat it. But people could use it for other purposes, such as greasing cart axles, waterproofing animal hides, and other household uses.
The command not to eat blood was very important. The Council at Jerusalem even included it in their instructions for non-Jewish (Gentile) believers ({{Acts 15:29|Acts 15:29}}).

*the breast of the wave offering and the thigh of the contribution of their peace offerings:* God, the priest, the worshiper, and guests shared this meal. Some translations call the breast a "wave offering" and the thigh the "contribution" or "heave offering." These were specifically for the priest (see {{Leviticus 10:13-15|Leviticus 10:13–15}}). After presenting these offerings in the tabernacle in front of the Lord, they ate them (see {{Exodus 29:24|Exodus 29:24}}, {{Exodus 29:26|26}}).

In {{Exodus 28:1-29:46|Exodus 28–29}}, the Lord gave Moses detailed instructions for clothing and ordaining Aaron and his sons as priests. In {{Exodus 39:1-31|Exodus 39:1–31}}; {{Exodus 40:12-16|40:12–16}}; and {{Leviticus 8:1-36|Leviticus 8}}, they followed these commands. Moses did not only tell them the instructions. He performed the ceremonies to show the priests exactly what to do, as the Lord had commanded him ({{Leviticus 8:9|8:9}}, {{Leviticus 8:13|13}}, {{Leviticus 8:17|17}}, {{Leviticus 8:21|21}}, {{Leviticus 8:29|29}}). Since disobedience could lead to death, God ensured the priests understood their duties clearly.

Aaron and his sons Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar were set apart as priests.

God had given clear instructions about how to do this in Exodus chapters 28 and 29. The ceremony included washing with special water and putting on the priests’ clothes. It included being anointed with oil and being sprinkled with blood from the sacrifices.

After seven days, Aaron and his sons started their work as priests. God was very pleased that they obeyed him completely. God showed his glory to the whole community and sent fire upon the altar. This filled the people with joy.

The main work of priests was to offer sacrifices and to teach the people. They were to tell the difference between what was holy and what was common. But Nadab and Abihu didn’t do that. They made an offering that went against what God had commanded. Because of this the Lord sent fire that killed Nadab and Abihu.

- {{Exodus 29:1-3|Exodus 29:1–3}}, {{Exodus 29:7|7}}also mentions these items. 

- *garments: *See {{Exodus 28:1-43|Exodus 28}}. 

- The anointing oil had special ingredients that gave it a special smell. These included myrrh, cinnamon, cane, and cassia (dried flowers from the cinnamon tree) mixed into olive oil (see {{Exodus 30:22-33|Exodus 30:22–33}}). 

- *bull of the sin offering:* See {{Leviticus 4:3-12|Leviticus 4:3–12}}. 

- The first of the two rams was a whole burnt offering ({{Leviticus 8:18|8:18}}), while the second was a special ordination sacrifice ({{Leviticus 8:22|8:22}}). 

- *basket of unleavened bread:* See {{Leviticus 6:19-23|6:19–23}}.

The text repeatedly emphasizes that Moses did what the Lord instructed. He obeyed the commands God gave in {{Exodus 29:1-46|Exodus 29}} (see also {{Leviticus 8:9|Leviticus 8:9}}, {{Leviticus 8:13|13}}, {{Leviticus 8:17|17}}, {{Leviticus 8:21|21}}, {{Leviticus 8:29|29}}, {{Leviticus 8:36|36}}).

*washed them with water:* This was the first step to remove impurity. The priests needed to be ceremonially clean before serving the Lord in holiness ({{Exodus 29:4|Exodus 29:4}}; see {{Psalm 24:4|Psalm 24:4}}).

- The priestly tunic was woven from patterned linen cloth (see {{Exodus 28:39|Exodus 28:39}}). 

- The Israelites used same material for the tabernacle curtains as with the embroidered ephod (see {{Exodus 28:4|Exodus 28:4}}, {{Exodus 28:6-14|6–14}}). The exact shape and size of the ephod are not known, but it seems to have been a long, sleeveless vest. It fit closely to the body and tied at the waist. Gold settings joined it at the shoulders, each holding an onyx stone engraved with the names of six tribes of Israel ({{Exodus 28:9|Exodus 28:9}}). Later, an ephod also referred to a honored image ({{Judges 8:27|Judges 8:27}}; {{Judges 18:17|18:17}}). 

- They embroidered and made the decorative sash from the same materials as the ephod (see {{Exodus 28:8|Exodus 28:8}}).

- The breastpiece (see {{Exodus 28:15-30|Exodus 28:15–30}}) was made it from embroidered linen folded in half. It had twelve stones, each engraved with the name of an Israelite tribe. A gold chain from the gold shoulder pieces of the ephod held it over the chest. 

- The priests placed the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece pocket ({{Exodus 28:30|Exodus 28:30}}; {{1 Samuel 23:9-12|1 Samuel 23:9–12}}; {{1 Samuel 30:7-8|30:7–8}}). Their exact purpose is unclear. Most scholars think they are two stones, possibly different in color, that were cast as lots. They could give a positive, neutral, or negative answer to difficult questions ({{Exodus 28:30|Exodus 28:30}}; {{Numbers 27:21|Numbers 27:21}}; {{1 Samuel 28:6|1 Samuel 28:6}}). Their mention in later Old Testament prophetic writings shows how important these items were for the work of the priest ({{Ezra 2:63|Ezra 2:63}}; {{Nehemiah 7:65|Nehemiah 7:65}}).

The turban worn by the high priest was made of linen. It was different from the headdresses the common priests wore ({{Exodus 28:40|Exodus 28:40}}). A gold medallion hung from the turban. It had the words "HOLY TO THE LORD" inscribed on it ({{Exodus 28:36|Exodus 28:36}}). With the names of the tribes on his shoulders and over his heart and the dedication to the Lord on his forehead, the high priest was clearly marked as the people’s representative to God and God’s representative to the people. In this role, the high priest mediated for the people and modeled the standard for all priests.

*he consecrated them *(or *he made them holy*): God is "the Holy One" ({{Psalm 78:41|Psalm 78:41}}; {{Psalm 22:3|22:3}}). Only God can truly make a person or thing holy ({{Leviticus 20:8|Leviticus 20:8}}; {{Leviticus 21:15|21:15}}, {{Leviticus 21:23|23}}; {{Leviticus 22:9|22:9}}, {{Leviticus 22:16|16}}, {{Leviticus 22:32|32}}; {{Exodus 31:13|Exodus 31:13}}; see {{Hebrews 2:11|Hebrews 2:11}}). Moses poured the anointing oil on the tabernacle and everything in it. This action showed that God had chosen these objects and set them apart for worship (also in {{Leviticus 8:11|Leviticus 8:11}}, {{Leviticus 8:12|12}}, {{Leviticus 8:15|15}}).
To learn about the clothing of common priests, see {{Exodus 28:40-41|Exodus 28:40–41}}.

- *sin offering* (see {{Leviticus 4:3-12|4:3–12}}): They made two offerings for atonement: 

- the sin offering ({{Leviticus 8:14-17|8:14–17}}) and 

- the whole burnt offering ({{Leviticus 8:18-21|8:18–21}}). 

- By placing their hands on the bull's head (see {{Leviticus 1:4|1:4}}), Aaron and his sons identified themselves with the sacrifice (also in {{Leviticus 8:18|8:18}}, {{Leviticus 8:22|22}}).
Normally, the high priest performed these duties. Yet, priests could not ordain themselves. So, Moses, as God's representative, established the priesthood.
*ram for the burnt offering:* See the study note on Leviticus 1:10–13.

*Aaron's right earlobe … thumb … big toe: *These body parts represented the total person. This act emphasized the priest's role, with the blood stressing connections to the sacrificial system. The priest's main job was to mediate between God and his people. To do this well, he needed ears to hear God's words and his people's needs. He also needed hands ready to obey God's commands, and feet ready to go where needed.
Moses acted as a priest during the ordination ceremony, so he received the priest's portion of the offering (see {{Leviticus 8:15|Leviticus 8:15}}).
*anointing oil: *See the study note on Leviticus 8:2; see also {{Psalm 133:2|Psalm 133:2}}.

The ordination offering was a type of peace offering ({{Exodus 29:28|Exodus 29:28}}). It was a meal shared between God and the priests ({{Leviticus 7:11-18|Leviticus 7:11–18}}, {{Leviticus 7:28-34|28–34}}). The parts of the offering burned on the altar belonged to God. The command to boil and eat the ordination offerings first appears in {{Exodus 29:32|Exodus 29:32}}.

*commanded by the LORD:* The details of the sacrifice ceremonies were symbolic and important. But the most important part was for the priests to obey God's commands. Complete obedience to God is a major theme in both the Old Testament and the New Testament: “obedience is better than sacrifice” ({{1 Samuel 15:22|1 Samuel 15:22}}).

*seven days:* This command emphasized God's complete holiness and required strict obedience to his commands. The priests, now anointed as God's holy servants, had to stay in the tabernacle court for seven days before returning to daily life.

- *eighth day:* The priests completed the seven-day probation period as commanded in {{Leviticus 8:35|Leviticus 8:35}}. 

- *elders:* See the study note on Leviticus 4:15.

At the start of the priests' ministry, several sacrifices were required. The priests offered a sin offering and a whole burnt offering. The people offered a sin offering, a burnt offering, a peace offering, and a grain offering. These sacrifices made sure that all sin was atoned for and the covenant with God was affirmed. The only sacrifice not included was the guilt offering.

Just as *holiness* describes God's character, *the glory of the LORD* shows God's power and majesty (see {{Ezekiel 1:28|Ezekiel 1:28}}; {{Ezekiel 10:4|10:4}}). God's glory appeared:

- on Mount Sinai ({{Exodus 24:16|Exodus 24:16}}), 

- at the dedication of the tabernacle ({{Exodus 40:34-35|Exodus 40:34–35}}), and 

- in Solomon's temple ({{1 Kings 8:11|1 Kings 8:11}}; {{2 Chronicles 7:1|2 Chronicles 7:1}}). 

But God's glory also fills the heavens ({{Psalm 19:1|Psalm 19:1}}). 

The New Testament describes Christ's glory as the image of God ({{2 Corinthians 4:4|2 Corinthians 4:4}}), who showed God's glory to the world ({{John 1:14|John 1:14}}). God glorified Christ in his death and resurrection ({{John 17:1-5|John 17:1–5}}). See also {{Exodus 24:15-17|Exodus 24:15–17}}.
*your sin offering and your burnt offering:* Before the high priest could make atonement for the people, he first had to be right with God himself.

- Both Aaron, the high priest , and his sons, the common priests, took part in the sin offering and the burnt offering ({{Leviticus 9:8-14|Leviticus 9:8–14}}). Their shared work made atonement effective for the whole priesthood.

- *horns of the altar:* See study note on Leviticus 4:25; see also {{Exodus 27:1-8|Exodus 27:1–8}}.
*the morning’s burnt offering:* They offered a lamb as a whole burnt offering each morning and evening ({{Leviticus 6:9|Leviticus 6:9}}; {{Numbers 28:2-4|Numbers 28:2–4}}).

*Fire came out from the presence of the LORD: *This showed that God accepted the offerings, the atonement, and the priesthood ({{Leviticus 9:7|Leviticus 9:7}}; compare {{1 Kings 18:36-38|1 Kings 18:36–38}}).

- Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu ({{Exodus 6:23|Exodus 6:23}}): These were Aaron's oldest sons who had gone with Moses and the seventy elders to Mount Sinai ({{Exodus 24:1|Exodus 24:1}}, {{Exodus 24:9|9}}). They also saw the great theophany (appearance of God) there. They died without male children (see also {{Exodus 28:1|Exodus 28:1}}; {{Numbers 3:2-4|Numbers 3:2–4}}; {{Numbers 26:60-61|26:60–61}}; {{1 Chronicles 6:3|1 Chronicles 6:3}}; {{1 Chronicles 24:1-2|24:1–2}}). 

- *censers:* These were fire pans or trays for holding hot coals. They sprinkled incense on them ({{Exodus 30:34-38|Exodus 30:34–38}}; see also {{Leviticus 16:12-13|Leviticus 16:12–13}}; {{2 Chronicles 26:19|2 Chronicles 26:19}}; {{Revelation 8:3-4|Revelation 8:3–4}}). 

- *unauthorized fire: *The Hebrew phrase *’esh zarah *means “strange fire.” This could mean “foreign,” and thus “unauthorized” (see {{Exodus 30:9|Exodus 30:9}}) or even “pagan” (as in {{Psalm 44:20|Psalm 44:20}}; {{Psalm 81:9|81:9}}). 

It seems that Nadab and Abihu used fire from a source not approved by God ({{Numbers 3:4|Numbers 3:4}}; {{Numbers 26:61|26:61}}). It could have been even a pagan source. They might have offered incense not prepared according to God's instructions ({{Exodus 30:34-38|Exodus 30:34–38}}).{{Exodus 30:34-38|Exodus 30:34-38}}The text does not mention that though. They entered God’s presence in their own way, not his.

A fire was to burn all the time on the bronze altar. Its coals were to be used for burning incense ({{Leviticus 6:9|Leviticus 6:9}}; {{Leviticus 16:12|16:12}}). Nadab and Abihu, perhaps careless because they had been drinking wine ({{Leviticus 10:8-11|10:8–11}}), took coals from another place. This broke God’s command, and they died as a result.

In {{Leviticus 9:24|Leviticus 9:24}}, the fire showed God's acceptance. Now, it shows his disapproval by causing the death of Nadab and Abihu. They had shown a careless attitude toward worshiping God (compare {{Acts 5:1-11|Acts 5:1–11}}).
God's holiness is central to his character, different from the world of creatures. By acting recklessly, Nadab and Abihu ignored God's holiness and did not honor him.

- *Mishael and Elzaphan…uncle Uzziel:* See {{Exodus 6:18|Exodus 6:18}}, {{Exodus 6:22|22}}. 

- *carry the bodies of your cousins: *Aaron, the high priest, and the priests Eleazar and Ithamar could not touch a dead person because it would make them ceremonially unclean ({{Leviticus 10:6|Leviticus 10:6}};{{Leviticus 10:6|Leviticus 10:6}}{{Leviticus 21:10-12|21:10–12}}).
They carried the bodies by their clothes to avoid contamination.

- *Eleazar and Ithamar* were Aaron’s two remaining sons ({{Exodus 6:23|Exodus 6:23}}). 

- *let your hair become disheveled:* In biblical times, this and similar practices showed grief (see {{Genesis 37:29|Genesis 37:29}}; {{Genesis 44:13|44:13}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:1|Deuteronomy 14:1}}; {{2 Samuel 1:11|2 Samuel 1:11}}; {{Job 1:20|Job 1:20}}; {{Jeremiah 16:6|Jeremiah 16:6}}; {{Jeremiah 47:5|47:5}}). As high priest, Aaron could not participate in these ceremonies or show his grief ({{Leviticus 21:10|Leviticus 21:10}}). This rule also applied to Eleazar and Ithamar. If God’s representatives had shown grief, people might have thought they disagreed with God’s justice. But the common people were allowed to mourn.

- Eleazar and Ithamar could not attend the funeral. 

- *the LORD’s anointing oil:* They had recently become priests (see {{Leviticus 7:36|Leviticus 7:36}}), so they had to avoid any contact with the dead.

- The placement of this instruction suggests that Nadab and Abihu might have been drinking alcohol when they offered the "unauthorized fire" ({{Leviticus 10:1|Leviticus 10:1}}). Priests should not drink anything that could impair their judgment before serving in the tabernacle. 

- *the Lord said to Aaron:* Previously, God communicated only with Moses, but now he accepted Aaron as the people's representative and spoke directly to him. 

- The word *common* means "secular" or "ordinary." 

- *clean and the unclean:* See {{Leviticus 7:19-21|Leviticus 7:19–21}}; {{Leviticus 11:1-15:33|11:1–15:33}}.
God's decrees were laws given directly by God, not decided by a human court.

- *the grain offering: *This was part of the ordination ceremony (see {{Leviticus 8:26|Leviticus 8:26}}; {{Exodus 29:2|Exodus 29:2}}, {{Exodus 29:23|23}}). 

- *without leaven beside the altar, because it is most holy:* Moses wanted to be certain no fermentation had occurred in the priest's portion of the grain offering ({{Leviticus 6:14-18|Leviticus 6:14–18}}).

The priest's share of the grain, sin, and guilt offerings was "most holy" (see {{Leviticus 2:3|Leviticus 2:3}}; {{Leviticus 6:29|6:29}}; {{Leviticus 7:6|7:6}}). Only the males in the priest's family could eat it. They had to eat it in a holy place, like the tabernacle court. Yet, the priest's portion of the peace offering was only "holy." Any family member could eat it in any clean place ({{Leviticus 22:10-13|22:10–13}}).

The goat of the sin offering was the offering for the people ({{Leviticus 9:3|Leviticus 9:3}}, {{Leviticus 9:15-17|15–17}}; compare {{Leviticus 9:2|9:2}}, {{Leviticus 9:8-11|8–11}}). On this special occasion, the priests did not take the blood into the Holy Place as usually required. After offering the parts meant for God, the priests should have eaten the remaining portion (see {{Leviticus 6:29|6:29}}). But they burned the entire goat, even though its blood had not entered the sanctuary ({{Leviticus 10:18|10:18}}; see {{Leviticus 6:30|6:30}}).

*Since these things have happened to me: *Aaron may have meant two things. He could have been saying that eating the goat of the sin offering would not have stopped the deaths of Nadab and Abihu. Or he may have meant that it was not right for him to eat it immediately after such a painful event.

The laws in these chapters were about food, having babies and skin diseases. They were also about mould and liquid waste from people’s bodies.

There were two main points with these laws in Leviticus. The first was that the Israelites were to be different from other people groups. The foods they were allowed to eat and those they weren’t allowed to eat showed this. Being different showed that the Israelites didn’t follow the false gods of other people groups. They followed the true God who was holy.

The second main point was that God is the God of life. Death is the result of sin. God doesn’t want sin and death to be in the world that he created. So things that had to do with death made people unclean. God’s people received rules from him about how to be considered clean and pure. Being clean and pure allowed them to worship God together with the community.

These chapters explain the rules about purity. Mixing different types of animals was forbidden (see {{Deuteronomy 22:9-11|Deuteronomy 22:9–11}}). This is because it opposed God's natural order. Creatures like fish without fins and scales, meat-eating animals, crawling insects, and animals without split hooves were considered "abnormal." They crossed the boundaries between "normal" types and were not suitable for food or offerings (see also {{Deuteronomy 14:1-21|Deuteronomy 14:1–21}}). The dietary laws intended to set Israel apart as a holy people from other nations ({{Leviticus 11:44-45|Leviticus 11:44–45}}).
*these ones you may eat:* The Israelites considered animals with split hooves that chew cud to be "normal" and ceremonially clean (see also {{Deuteronomy 14:3-21|Deuteronomy 14:3–21}}).

Some scholars think people avoided ceremonially unclean animals for health reasons. But evidence does not support this suggestion. Horse meat, for instance, is as healthy as beef, yet it was "unclean" because the horse does not have a split hoof (see {{Leviticus 11:2-3|Leviticus 11:2–3}}). These rules existed because an unclean animal was not suitable as an offering to God. So, it was likewise not suitable as food for God's people. 

Jesus proclaimed all foods clean for Christians ({{Mark 7:14-19|Mark 7:14–19}}). This teaching was confirmed in Peter’s vision ({{Acts 10:9-16|Acts 10:9–16}}).
The rock badger and the rabbit do not actually chew cud, even though it looks like they do. They are ceremonially unclean because they lack split hooves.
*the creatures that live in the water:* The Israelites considered animals from the water to be clean (acceptable for food and for ritual use) only if they had both fins and scales
The prohibition included fish like eels and sharks, which have fins but no scales. It also included crustaceans and mollusks, which have neither fins nor scales.

The list of ceremonially unclean birds includes birds of prey and scavengers. These birds often touch dead animals and blood, making them unclean and unfit for eating and offerings. Bats fly but are not birds ({{Leviticus 11:19|Leviticus 11:19}}). So, they are "abnormal" and ceremonially unclean.

*insects that walk on all fours: those having jointed legs above their feet:* This phrase excludes creatures that creep or crawl close to the ground ({{Leviticus 11:27|Leviticus 11:27}}). {{Leviticus 11:42|Leviticus 11:42}} says that creatures with many legs, like centipedes, are ceremonially unclean. Locusts and grasshoppers are examples of ceremonially clean insects (see {{Matthew 3:4|Matthew 3:4}}).
*unclean until evening:* Anyone who touched a ceremonially unclean animal that was dead would be unclean until evening. In Israel, evening marked the start of the next day.

This list of ceremonially unclean creatures that crawl includes both warm-blooded and cold-blooded animals that move along the ground. Snakes are also part of this group ({{Leviticus 11:42|Leviticus 11:42}}).

Dead animals could make objects and people ceremonially unclean. Even a ceremonially clean animal that died without its blood drained was unclean ({{Leviticus 11:39-40|Leviticus 11:39–40}}). If a person touched the body of a dead animal, they were unclean until evening. Household items that touched the body of a dead animal needed purification or the people had to destroy the items ({{Leviticus 11:25|11:25}}, {{Leviticus 11:28|28}}, {{Leviticus 11:32|32}}, {{Leviticus 11:40|40}}; {{Leviticus 11:33|11:33}}, {{Leviticus 11:35|35}}).
A cistern was a hole dug into the ground or rock. They often lined it with plaster to hold rain and surface water.

People probably moistened grain with water to cook it for food. Eating contaminated grain was like eating a dead animal. But if they planted the grain, the new plant and its grain were ceremonially clean.

Israelites could not consume blood ({{Leviticus 7:26|Leviticus 7:26}}). They could eat an animal only after draining and properly disposing of the blood ({{Leviticus 17:13|17:13}}). If a ceremonially clean animal died naturally and did not have its blood drained, it became ceremonially unclean. An Israelite could give or sell such an animal to foreigners but could not eat it ({{Deuteronomy 14:21|Deuteronomy 14:21}}).

- *I am the LORD your God:* See study note on Leviticus 18:2. 

- *be holy, because I am holy:* These words express the main theme of Leviticus: God is holy. They must consider and treat God as holy. God expects holiness from his people ({{Leviticus 10:3|Leviticus 10:3}}; {{Leviticus 19:2|19:2}}). This verse teaches that God's character influences those who make a covenant with him (see also {{Leviticus 11:45|11:45}}; {{Leviticus 20:7|20:7}}, {{Leviticus 20:26|26}}; {{Leviticus 21:8|21:8}}, {{Leviticus 21:15|15}}; {{Leviticus 22:9|22:9}}, {{Leviticus 22:16|16}}, {{Leviticus 22:32|32}}). They must become holy in their actions ({{Exodus 22:31|Exodus 22:31}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:9|Deuteronomy 28:9}}; compare {{1 Peter 1:16|1 Peter 1:16}}).

*brought you up out of the land of Egypt: *This phrase or a similar one appears often in the first five books of the Bible (see {{Leviticus 19:36|Leviticus 19:36}}; {{Leviticus 22:33|22:33}}; {{Leviticus 25:38|25:38}}; {{Leviticus 26:13|26:13}}; {{Exodus 13:9|Exodus 13:9}}; {{Exodus 20:2|20:2}}; {{Numbers 15:41|Numbers 15:41}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:37|Deuteronomy 4:37}}). Each time, it reminds the Israelites, God's chosen people, of God's great act of freeing them from Egypt. Other verses in the Old Testament often mention the exodus event ({{Psalm 80:8|Psalms 80:8}}; {{Psalm 106:21|106:21}}; {{Isaiah 11:16|Isaiah 11:16}}; {{Jeremiah 34:13|Jeremiah 34:13}}; {{Hosea 12:9|Hosea 12:9}}; {{Hosea 13:4|13:4}}; {{Amos 2:10|Amos 2:10}}).

These verses explain the rules about childbirth. Any bodily discharge, including blood, was "abnormal" because it weakened the person and made them ceremonially unclean (see study notes on Leviticus 5:3; 11:1–15:33). These verses focus on the discharge that comes with childbirth, not childbirth itself ({{Leviticus 12:2|12:2}}, {{Leviticus 12:5|5}}, {{Leviticus 12:7|7}}). The uncleanness was not sinful unless they ignored it and it came into contact with something holy (see {{Leviticus 5:2-3|5:2–3}}).
By the eighth day, a baby’s body has developed enough for blood to clot well. This made circumcision safer at that time.
These thirty-three days, plus the previous seven days mentioned in {{Leviticus 12:2|Leviticus 12:2}}, {{Leviticus 12:3|3}} make a total of forty days for the mother's period of purification.
*two weeks … sixty-six days:* The total is eighty days. This is double the purification time needed for a son's birth (see also {{Leviticus 27:2-7|Leviticus 27:2–7}}).

*sin offering:* The Hebrew word is the same as the* sin offering* (*khatta’t*, see study note on Leviticus 4:1–5:13). Some scholars think this offering was only for *purification* or decontamination, including cases mentioned in {{Leviticus 5:1-6|Leviticus 5:1–6}}. 

This offering here was part of a *purification* ceremony. But it is more probable that the* sin offering* addressed a lack or failure. In this context, the focus is on purity rather than sin. It is meant to restore the woman to community fellowship, not to forgive a sinner.
*make atonement for her: *Here “atonement” means ceremonial cleansing and making peace between the worshiper and God (see {{Leviticus 4:20|Leviticus 4:20}}; also refer to study note on 1:4).
*cannot afford a lamb:* The alternative offering is for the poorer members of society (see {{Leviticus 5:7-13|Leviticus 5:7–13}}; compare {{Luke 2:22-24|Luke 2:22–24}}).

*a skin disease*: The Hebrew word *tsaraʿat* refers to more than Hansen’s disease (leprosy), which is rare and severely disfiguring. In Leviticus, the word describes many different conditions. These include:

- an open sore ({{Leviticus 13:10|13:10}}), 

- a boil ({{Leviticus 13:18|13:18}}), 

- a burn ({{Leviticus 13:24|13:24}}), 

- a sore on the head or chin ({{Leviticus 13:29|13:29}}), 

- shiny white patches ({{Leviticus 13:38|13:38}}), or 

- unusual baldness ({{Leviticus 13:40|13:40}}). 

A key test was whether the condition spread to other parts of the body ({{Leviticus 13:5-8|13:5–8}}). If it did, they quarantined the person while the disorder lasted ({{Leviticus 13:46|13:46}}). Not only people, but also clothing and even buildings could become infected ({{Leviticus 13:47-59|13:47–59}}; {{Leviticus 14:33-53|14:33–53}}).

Regarding regulations for infections, the idea of "normal" and "abnormal" is important (see “Clean, Unclean, and Holy” Theme Note). Infections in people, clothing, or buildings are not normal. They indicate disease and death. This is the opposite of wholeness. So, infections make a person ceremonially unclean.

- Skin disorders that could become contagious required precautions to stop their spread. These included swelling, rashes, or discolored skin. Until healed, the person was ceremonially unclean. The diseases mentioned here had a broad range. These included allergic rash, ringworm, or eczema, as well as serious conditions like gangrene. In Old Testament times, people diagnosed skin conditions by observation. Priests served in religious and medical roles. 

- *one of his sons: *These priestly duties were meant for future generations of priests too.

*deeper than the skin:* This means the infection either damaged the skin or was visible under it. The white hair and the skin depression showed a skin disease that could spread ({{Leviticus 13:21-23|Leviticus 13:21–23}}). This made the person ceremonially unclean ({{Leviticus 13:8|13:8}}).
The main purpose of isolating someone was to find out if a person was sick. It gave the priest time to watch the person’s symptoms.
If the rash spread, the priest declared the person unclean, and the isolation became long-term.
The key factor was the presence of an open sore, because it showed that there was an infection.

The completely white skin might mean a loss of pigment (see also {{Leviticus 13:3|Leviticus 13:3}}). Raw flesh showed infection and ceremonial uncleanness ({{Leviticus 13:10|13:10}}, {{Leviticus 13:14|14}}).

- The priest needed to check the burned area to see if there was an infection in the wound (see {{Leviticus 13:9-17|Levticus 13:9–17}}). 

- *hair … has turned white:* See {{Leviticus 13:18-23|13:18–23}}.
The *scaly outbreak* indicated a fungal infection in the scalp or beard, hidden by hair. Symptoms included hair loss and crusty skin.

If a skin rash had pus or swelling, it was probably an infection ({{Leviticus 13:42|Leviticus 13:42}}). If it only appeared as a white area, it was probably vitiligo (leucoderma). This harmless condition causes patches of skin to lose color.
A *reddish-white sore* may have shown signs of pus (a thick fluid from infection) and swelling.

- People often tore their clothing, left their hair uncombed, and covered their mouths to show they were mourning ({{Leviticus 10:6|Leviticus 10:6}}). 

- *Unclean, unclean!: *This cry indicated both social rejection and a health risk. It warned others that the person's skin disorder might be contagious and that holy items should not touch the ceremonially unclean person.

The tabernacle, which held the ark of the covenant, was at the center of the camp. This was so the people would know God was present there ({{Deuteronomy 23:14|Deuteronomy 23:14}}). If someone had a skin disorder, they had to live alone in a place outside the camp. This prevented the spread of infection and kept holy things cermonially clean. 

Even Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, spent seven days outside the camp ({{Numbers 12:15|Numbers 12:15}}). This area was not just for those with skin disorders. They also burned uneaten sin offerings ({{Leviticus 4:21|Lev 4:21}}) and executed criminals there ({{Leviticus 24:14|24:14}}, {{Leviticus 24:23|23}}). They took dead bodies there to keep the living area ceremonially clean ({{Leviticus 10:4-5|10:4–5}}). People also took care of bodily functions outside the camp ({{Deuteronomy 23:12-14|Deuteronomy 23:12–14}}).
*mildew:* This word refers to different types of molds or mildews that could spread on cloth or leather.

In Israel, the rainy season lasts from mid-October through March, bringing humid and cool weather. Mildew thrives during this period. Its spores can cause severe allergic reactions, creating a health issue. 

The rules for mildew in clothing were like those for infections in people. If the mildew spread, it was serious. If they could stop, wash, or cut it out, they could save the garment. This process was also similar to treating rot and mold in buildings ({{Leviticus 14:33-53|Leviticus 14:33–53}}).
To fully understand these verses about purifying infected people, read them with {{Leviticus 13:1-46|Leviticus 13:1–46}}.

The items listed here were part of the cleansing ceremony with the ashes of the red heifer ({{Numbers 19:6|Numbers 19:6}}). Their exact significance is unclear (see also {{Hebrews 9:18-22|Hebrews 9:18–22}}). *Hyssop* was a small plant used for sprinkling blood and in purification rites ({{Exodus 12:22|Exodus 12:22}}; {{Numbers 19:18|Numbers 19:18}}).

Killing the bird and sprinkling its blood ({{Leviticus 14:7|Leviticus 14:7}}) is similar to {{Exodus 24:6-8|Exodus 24:6–8}}. This is where Moses sprinkled all of Israel with blood to establish them as God's covenant community. In these verses, they cleansed the individual by sprinkling them with blood and allowed them to return to the community. They also used fresh water in cleansing ceremonies and in preparing sacrifices ({{Numbers 8:7|Numbers 8:7}}; {{Leviticus 1:9|Leviticus 1:9}}, {{Leviticus 1:13|13}}).

The goat released to Azazel symbolized removing sin from the community on the Day of Atonement ({{Leviticus 16:10|Leviticus 16:10}}, {{Leviticus 16:20-22|20–22}}). In a similar way, releasing the live bird symbolized removing an individual's ceremonial uncleanness.

The *guilt offering *was also sometimes called the "penalty" or "reparation" offering. It was for those who were ceremonially unclean and lived outside the camp. They could not bring sacrifices, tithes, and offerings while unclean (see {{Leviticus 5:14-16|Leviticus 5:14–16}}).
*the right earlobe … thumb … big toe: *These symbolized what a person hears, does, and where they go (also {{Leviticus 14:17|Leviticus 14:17}}, {{Leviticus 14:28|28}}; see study note on 8:23).

In the ancient world, people often used olive oil to help with healing (see {{Isaiah 1:6|Isaiah 1:6}}; {{Luke 10:34|Luke 10:34}}). Its use here might symbolize healing and cleansing of the infection. This allowed the person to rejoin the community. It may also have represented a restored connection between God, the priest, and the worshiper.

- This *sin offering *was the purification offering mentioned in {{Leviticus 12:6|Leviticus 12:6}} (see {{Leviticus 4:2-3|4:2–3}}). 

- *burnt offering: *This atoned for sins committed during the time of ceremonial uncleanness when the person could not bring offerings (see {{Leviticus 1:4|1:4}}).
*grain offering:* See study note on Leviticus 2:1–16.
The ceremony for the poor was similar to the usual purification offering. But, it allowed them to use cheaper birds instead of a lamb (see {{Leviticus 5:7-13|Leviticus 5:7–13}}).

Rot or mildew contamination made buildings unhealthy or unsafe. People considered these buildings diseased, so they were not whole or ceremonially clean (see study note on Leviticus 11:1–15:33). The inspection and treatment process was similar to the process for mildew in clothing ({{Leviticus 13:47-59|Leviticus 13:47–59}}).

*I put a contamination:* Biblical language reflects belief in one God who rules over everything. This means God is described as causing or allowing all events. For example, {{Exodus 21:13|Exodus 21:13}} describes an accidental death as something God allowed (see also {{Deuteronomy 19:4-5|Deuteronomy 19:4–5}}).
When a house was emptied, it showed that the house was not considered unclean until the priest said it was. The owner removed the furniture so that it would not be included in the quarantine period.

If mildew spread deeper than the wall’s surface, it was more serious than mildew only on the surface. A similar idea was used in examining people with skin disease. The priest looked to see if the disease went deeper than the skin (see study note on Leviticus 13:3).
This is a summary statement about many kinds of infections (compare {{Leviticus 11:46-47|Leviticus 11:46–47}}).

The idea of normal and abnormal, along with the created order, helps interpret these rules (see “Clean, Unclean, and Holy” Theme Note). Bodily discharges, like infections (see study note on Leviticus 13:1–46), were not considered "normal" because they weakened a person's health. This made the person seem incomplete. Whether male ({{Leviticus 15:1-18|15:1–18}}) or female ({{Leviticus 15:19-33|15:19–33}}), such a person became unclean.

*bodily discharge* (literally *a flowing from his flesh*): Most scholars think the word *flesh* refers to sexual organs, suggesting an infection like gonorrhea. Others believe it might mean a *discharge* of semen or even diarrhea. But a *discharge* of semen is improbable because it is specifically mentioned in {{Leviticus 15:16-17|Leviticus 15:16–17}} and only requires washing with water. It is clear that this *bodily discharge* came from "under him" ({{Leviticus 15:10|15:10}}). It contaminated anything he sat on or lay upon ({{Leviticus 15:4|15:4}}, {{Leviticus 15:6|6}}, {{Leviticus 15:9|9}}).

Unlike the man with a skin disease, a man with a bodily discharge could stay at home (see {{Leviticus 13:46|Leviticus 13:46}}). He did not need the detailed cleansing ceremony described in chapter {{Leviticus 14:1-57|14}}. He only had to wait seven days after the discharge stopped, wash ({{Leviticus 15:13|15:13}}), and offer two birds as sacrifices. One was a sin offering and the other was a whole burnt offering.

In the case of an emission of semen, the discharge was not a sign of illness (see study note on Leviticus 15:1–33). But the same rule applied. The man had to wash and was ceremonially unclean until the next evening.

If a man had a seminal emission during sexual intercourse, both he and the woman became unclean. They had to wash and remain unclean until evening. This was because of a natural bodily emission, not because of infection or disease, and no sacrifice was required.

A woman's menstrual period is natural and not a disease. But because it involved a bloody discharge, she became ceremonially unclean (see {{Leviticus 15:32-33|Leviticus 15:32–33}}). The rules were similar to those for a man with a bodily discharge ({{Leviticus 15:2-12|15:2–12}}). She could stay at home, but anything she sat on became unclean. Anyone who touched her had to wash, and she probably did the same after the seven-day quarantine. There was no animal sacrifice needed.

Sexual intercourse with a woman during her menstrual period will later be forbidden and will have a harsh penalty ({{Leviticus 18:19|Leviticus 8:19}}). This verse probably describes a situation where the woman's menstrual flow went unnoticed when the sexual activity started. Or it could be when her period began during intercourse. The rules required the man who came into contact with her blood to share the woman's seven-day quarantine.
