Normal menstruation did not require any offering from the woman ({{Leviticus 15:19-24|Leviticus 15:19–24}}). If a woman had a discharge of blood lasting more than seven days, she needed a cleansing ceremony. This was similar to the one for a man cleansed of a bodily discharge ({{Leviticus 15:13-15|15:13–15}}; see also {{Matthew 9:20-22|Matthew 9:20–22}}).
This is a summary of the principles in {{Leviticus 15:1-31|Leviticus 15:1–31}}. Bodily discharges made a person ceremonially unclean. This included pus, semen, menstrual fluid, or blood.

God provided guilt offerings and sin offerings to deal with sin. These offerings helped the Israelites understand that their sins were forgiven.

But the places where the Israelites lived were made unclean because of their sins. This was true of the whole camp. It was also true of the holy tent and the Most Holy Room. If those places stayed impure and unclean, God could not be present there.

So God provided a way for the Israelites to be made pure and clean. This happened once a year on the Day of Atonement. This was the day when sins were paid for. When someone pays for their sin, it means that they atone for their sin.

The Day of Atonement involved live goats. One goat was sacrificed. The high priest would say out loud to God the sins of the Israelites. He would talk about this while his hands were on the other goat’s head. This was a sign of passing the sins from the people onto the goat. Then the goat would be led out into the desert. This was a sign of the sins being taken far away from the people.

Many years later, Jesus took all sin on himself. He sacrificed himself as a sin offering. In this way he was like the goats. He took away sin’s power over people. All who believe in him are made clean and pure for ever. No other sacrifices are needed to pay for the sin of those who believe in Jesus.

The day of atonement, on the tenth day of the seventh month, was the most serious and holy day of the year for Israelites (see {{Leviticus 16:29|Leviticus 16:29}}; {{Leviticus 23:27|23:27}}; {{Numbers 29:7|Numbers 29:7}}). It was the only required fast and a Sabbath of rest for all the people ({{Leviticus 23:32|Leviticus 23:32}}). The Feast of Trumpets came before it and announced its arrival ({{Numbers 29:1|Numbers 29:1}}, {{Numbers 29:7-11|7–11}}). On this day, God forgave the sins of the community. Only the high priest, Aaron, could lead the ceremony because he represented all the people. This included Aaron’s sons, the other priests. Today, the Jews call the day of atonement Yom Kippur.

A veil separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. The sanctuary was like God's palace. The Most Holy Place was his throne room, and the ark was his throne (see {{Leviticus 1:1|Leviticus 1:1}}). In the ancient Near East, entering a king's presence without an invitation could mean death ({{Esther 4:11|Esther 4:11}}). 

So, Aaron could not enter the Most Holy Place informally. Even the high priest could not enter. The only exception was when God required his presence for the Day of Atonement ceremony.

During the Day of Atonement ceremony, the high priest wore simple linen clothes instead of his usual robes. This probably symbolized the humility everyone should have on this solemn day. The high priest stood in front of God as the representative of the people. But he had nothing to boast about for himself or them. But when he stood in front of the people for God, his official robes showed God's glory and splendor ({{Leviticus 16:23|Leviticus 16:23}}).

The New Testament writer of the Letter to the Hebrews compares Aaron's work for Israel to Christ's work for believers. Both provided atonement for their people. Aaron had to offer a sacrifice for himself before he could offer a sin offering for the people to ensure God forgave his own sins ({{Hebrews 5:1-3|Hebrews 5:1–3}}). But Christ did not sin, though tempted ({{Hebrews 4:15|Hebrews 4:15}}). So, as the high priest for all Christians, he did not need to make a similar sacrifice ({{Hebrews 7:26-28|Hebrews 7:26–28}}).

The high priest had to purify *the Most Holy Place* and the rest of the Tent of Meeting. Throughout the year, the sins of the Israelites made the whole sanctuary ceremonially unclean. To keep the Tent of Meeting as a place to encounter God in the coming year, it needed purification. The same was true for the altar ({{Leviticus 16:18|Leviticus 16:18}}).

For this ceremony, the high priest had to wear special clothing used only for this purpose ({{Leviticus 16:4|Leviticus 16:4}}). When the ceremony ended, he had to leave the garments in the Most Holy Place. Many scholars believe that bathing and changing clothes were necessary because handling the sin offering caused ceremonial uncleanness.

On the day of atonement, the high priest brought the blood of the sin offerings* into the Most Holy Place*. Because of this, they burned the offerings completely instead of eating them ({{Leviticus 4:3-21|Leviticus 4:3–21}}).

- *you shall humble yourselves: *The Hebrew word is *‘anah*, which means "to humble" or "to afflict yourselves." In practice, this word is closely connected with fasting ({{Isaiah 58:3|Isaiah 58:3}}, {{Isaiah 58:5|5}}). 

- *foreigner*: The Hebrew word is *gēr*. It refers to people who were not Israelites but lived among them. Foreigners sometimes joined in Israel’s worship (see {{Numbers 9:14|Numbers 9:14}}). They probably did not own land but worked as day laborers, share-croppers, or tenant farmers. But if they lived among the Israelites, they had to follow Israelite laws and customs (see, for example, {{Leviticus 24:16|Leviticus 24:16}}).
The Israelites considered the day of atonement to be a Sabbath day. No one in the camp, whether Israelite or foreigner, could work (see {{Leviticus 19:30|Leviticus 19:30}}).

God set Israel apart from the other nations to be his own people. They weren’t to follow the practices of the people groups around them. They were to follow the practices God gave them. These practices would help God’s people be set apart and holy like God is.

There were rules about many things. The basis for all of them was how holy God is. There were rules about animals and their blood. There were rules about sex and making animal sacrifices. There were rules for how priests and the high priest were to behave. There were rules about how to treat other Israelites and outsiders.

The most important rule about how to treat others is in Leviticus 19:18. The Israelites were to love their neighbours as they loved themselves. This law was to guide them in every situation.

This section explains how the people of Israel were to live in holiness. Holiness is not just one quality of God. It describes all that God is—his person, nature, and character (see study note on Exodus 3:5). 

God's "glory" demonstrates his holiness (see {{Leviticus 9:6|Leviticus 9:6}}). God's covenant with Israel meant the people and the nation shared in God's holiness. This holiness relied on Israel's relationship with God. This relationship required Israel to meet certain ethical and ceremonial standards.

These rules show that unsupervised sacrifices could lead a mixture of pagan practices with true worship of the Lord (see also {{Deuteronomy 12:15-21|Deuteronomy 12:15–21}}; {{Leviticus 17:7|Leviticus 17:7}}). Israel camped around the Tent of Meeting so it was easy to bring an animal to the sanctuary for slaughter (see also {{Deuteronomy 12:15-21|Deuteronomy 12:15–21}}). {{Deuteronomy 12:20-24|Deuteronomy 12:20–24}} anticipates Israel settling in the land and the challenges of this rule. It allowed slaughtering and eating meat without bringing it to the sanctuary, as long as they did not consume the blood.

- *that man shall incur bloodguilt:* This person unlawfully killed an animal. God gave the animal life, and its blood must return to him through sacrifice. 

- *cut off: *See study note on Leviticus 7:20–21.

- *have prostituted themselves* (Hebrew *zanah*, which means "commit fornication"): Israel must worship only the Lord ({{Exodus 20:3|Exodus 20:3}}). Israel's covenant with the LORD was like a marriage (see {{Hosea 1:2|Hosea 1:2}}). Worshiping other gods was like spiritual adultery. 

Many Canaanite religions were fertility cults. This verb refers to prostitution at Canaanite pagan worship shrines. They believed these acts would make the land fertile through magic rites involving sexual intercourse. 

- The Hebrew word for *goat demons* is the plural form of "a male *goat*." In ancient times, the male *goat* symbolized fertility or a god of the underworld. During King Jeroboam I's reign, many Levites from the northern kingdom moved to Jerusalem. The use of goats and bulls in northern worship shocked them ({{2 Chronicles 11:15-16|2 Chronicles 11:15–16}}).

*the life of the flesh is in the blood:* God forbade Israel to consume blood because it symbolized the life given by God ({{Leviticus 17:10|Leviticus 17:10}}). They set it aside as God's portion of each animal offering. God also designated the sacrificial blood as the way to atone. This means God's grace accepted the life of the animal in exchange for the life of the sinner. 

In the New Testament, the blood of Christ—representing his life freely given—provides eternal redemption for believers ({{Hebrews 9:12|Hebrews 9:12}}).

*cover it with dirt:* This rule stopped hunters from using an animal's blood for food. Like the blood in altar offerings, the blood of wild game also symbolized life. Uncovered blood was a sign of violent crime. Innocent blood defiled the land ({{Numbers 35:33|Numbers 35:33}}). It called out to God for justice ({{Genesis 4:10|Genesis 4:10}}; see {{Job 16:18|Job 16:18}}). 

Covering the blood of a killed animal gave it a symbolic burial. This showed respect for both the animal's life and for God, the giver of life. The burial showed that the life was returning to God. This was similar to how the priest poured out the blood at the altar during offerings.

An animal killed by a predator or that died naturally still had blood in its tissues. This made it ceremonially unclean and a possible source of ceremonial uncleanness ({{Leviticus 22:8|Leviticus 22:8}}). Israelites must throw such an animal to the dogs or give or sell it to a non-Israelite ({{Exodus 22:31|Exodus 22:31}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:21|Deuteronomy 14:21}}). 

If an Israelite ate an animal with undrained blood, he or she became ceremonially unclean. Then they had to wash in water. The uncleanness was not a sin, but ignoring it led to punishment.

Chapters {{Leviticus 18:1-30|18}} and {{Leviticus 20:1-27|20}}focus mainly on sexual matters. They warn Israel not to follow the practices of pagan peoples, whether in religion or in daily life. Between these chapters, chapter {{Leviticus 19:1-37|19}} urges the people to live holy lives in everyday situations.

Many Near Eastern treaties started with the ruler's name and titles. The phrase, "I am the LORD your God," names the great king, Yahweh (LORD), and gives his title, "your God" (see also {{Exodus 20:2|Exodus 20:2}}; {{Deuteronomy 5:6|Deuteronomy 5:6}}). These words briefly recalled Israel’s covenant with God and all it meant. By reminding the people they belonged to the Lord, these words demanded a response ({{Leviticus 11:44|Leviticus 11:44}}; {{Leviticus 18:4-5|18:4–5}}). {{Leviticus 18:1-30|Chapter 18}} starts and ends with these words, and they appear often throughout chapters {{Leviticus 19:1-26:46|19–26}}.

- *judgments … statutes:* The Bible anticipated that courts would interpret God's laws for different situations. These interpretations became case laws, known as *mishpatim* in Hebrew (see “statutes” in {{Leviticus 10:11|Leviticus 10:11}}). 

- Paul refers to these verses in {{Romans 10:5|Romans 10:5}} and {{Galatians 3:12|Galatians 3:12}}, where he contrasts living "based on faith” or “by the law.”

*to have sexual relations *(literally *to uncover the nakedness of*): Similar rules in chapter {{Leviticus 20:1-27|20}} of Leviticus use the Hebrew word *shakab* (which means “lie with”). This often indicates an improper sexual relationship.

- *She is your mother:* Incest was illegal because it disrupted families. The commands about this sin included close relatives, even if not related by blood. Incest was a serious crime because it caused competition and chaos in the family. It threatened home safety by breaking family intimacy and belonging. 

- The Bible directs this command to men, even if the woman was older, like a mother. Men, especially household leaders or firstborns, had more power. This power came with the duty to use it lawfully. Men were more often the sexual aggressors in illegal unions, though not always (for example, {{Genesis 39:6-18|Genesis 39:6–18}}).

*expose the nakedness of your father: *The Hebrew text equates having sexual relations with your mother or any of your father's wives to having sexual relations with him (compare {{Genesis 35:22|Genesis 35:22}}; {{Genesis 49:4|49:4}}; see also {{1 Corinthians 5:1|1 Corinthians 5:1}}). The husband and his wife "become one flesh" ({{Genesis 2:24|Genesis 2:24}}; compare {{Ephesians 5:29|Ephesians 5:29}}). These commands always emphasize honoring your parents ({{Leviticus 20:9|Leviticus 20:9}}; {{Exodus 20:12|Exodus 20:12}}). These commands extend to other family members (see also study note on Leviticus 20:17).
Sexual relations with a sister from both the same father and mother brought dishonor to both parents. Relations with a sister from only one parent brought dishonor to that parent.
*your father's sister … mother's sister:* These actions would dishonor your father or mother.
Having sexual relations with your aunt would dishonor your uncle. This would also bring dishonor to your father (see {{Leviticus 20:20|Leviticus 20:20}}).

Having sexual relations with your father's wife would dishonor your father. Similarly, having sexual relations with your daughter-in-law would dishonor your son. The law considered daughters-in-law the same as natural daughters ({{Exodus 21:9|Exodus 21:9}}; compare {{Genesis 38:1-30|Genesis 38:1–30}}).

Having sexual relations with your sister-in-law would be adulterous and would disgrace your brother. An exception was the law of levirate marriage (see {{Deuteronomy 25:5-10|Deuteronomy 25:5–10}}). This required a man to marry his brother’s widow to produce an heir who was considered the dead brother’s son.

Chapter {{Leviticus 18:1-30|18}} of Leviticus prohibited marrying a woman along with her daughter or granddaughter. This was to prevent family disruption. It would violate the intimacy of the family group by making a wife compete with a younger woman for her husband's love. The penalty for this act was death by burning ({{Leviticus 20:14|20:14}}).

The word *rival* (Hebrew *tsarah*) clearly describes the relationship between Leah and Rachel as well as Hannah and Peninnah ({{Genesis 29:16-30:24|Genesis 29:16–30:24}}; {{1 Samuel 1:6|1 Samuel 1:6}}). In both cases, the wives competed bitterly for their husband's attention.

- The Hebrew word translated as *defile yourself* can be more literally translated as *to become ceremonially unclean.* 

- In the Old Testament, sexual intercourse with a neighbor’s wife or any married woman was adultery. Breaking this law was punishable by death ({{Deuteronomy 22:22|Deuteronomy 22:22}}). Like incest, adultery threatened the integrity and security of the home and family. It violated the marriage covenant and divided the adulterer’s affection between his spouse and his mistress.

- *Molech* was the national god of the Ammonites ({{1 Kings 11:7|1 Kings 11:7}}). Later, Israel worshiped this god during times of turning away from their faith ({{2 Kings 23:10|2 Kings 23:10}}; {{Jeremiah 32:35|Jeremiah 32:35}}). *Molech* worship probably appears here because it related to sexual sins and possibly included child sacrifice. 

- *profane* (or *blaspheme*) *the name of your God:* This meant using the name of the Lord as if it were unholy, such as in a false oath or in the worship of a false god ({{Leviticus 19:12|Leviticus 19:12}}; {{Ezekiel 20:39|Ezekiel 20:39}}).

In {{Genesis 1:31|Genesis 1:31}}, God declared all things good. This shows that what God creates and the way he designed it to work define what is good. One part of this good creation was the making of woman as a companion for man ({{Genesis 2:22-24|Genesis 2:22–24}}). Marriage reflects this design. It forms a small picture of the whole human race, which together bears God’s image. Sin entered the world through the original disobedience of humanity (called "the Fall") and disrupted this order ({{Genesis 3:1-24|Genesis 3}}). 

One example of this disruption is homosexuality. In {{Romans 1:25-32|Romans 1:25–32}}, Paul connects same-sex relations to the rejection of God by humanity that has turned away from him. The Hebrew word *to‘ebah *is often translated as"abomination." This word expresses strong disapproval and disgust ({{Leviticus 20:13|Leviticus 20:13}}; see also {{Leviticus 18:26-30|18:26–30}}).

- Like homosexuality, bestiality violates God's created order (see study note on Leviticus 18:22). 

- The Hebrew word for *perversion* refers not only to a violation but also to a confusion of the order God created. It destroys the clear boundaries that God established.

- *any of these practices:* 

- pagan worship ({{Leviticus 18:21|Leviticus 18:21}}),

- homosexuality ({{Leviticus 18:22|18:22}}), and

- bestiality ({{Leviticus 18:23|18:23}}). 

- The land could not endure the sinful practices of the Canaanites. It is described as vomiting them out, showing how completely they would be removed (see {{Leviticus 18:28|18:28}}).

Just as the land *spewed out* the Canaanites, it would also *vomit* the Israelites if they behaved like the Canaanites (see study note on Leviticus 18:24–25). This happened when the Assyrians destroyed and exiled the northern kingdom in 722 BC ({{2 Kings 17:6|2 Kings 17:6}}). This also happened when the Babylonians destroyed and exiled Judah in 586 BC ({{2 Kings 25:8-21|2 Kings 25:8–21}}).
*Be holy:* See study note on Leviticus 11:44–45.

*I am the LORD* (see {{Leviticus 18:2|Leviticus 18:2}}): These words divide chapter {{Leviticus 19:1-37|19}} into short, strong sections ({{Leviticus 19:3|19:3}}, {{Leviticus 19:4|4}}, {{Leviticus 19:10|10}}, {{Leviticus 19:12|12}}, {{Leviticus 19:14|14}}, {{Leviticus 19:16|16}}, {{Leviticus 19:18|18}}, {{Leviticus 19:25|25}}, {{Leviticus 19:28|28}}, {{Leviticus 19:30|30}}, {{Leviticus 19:31|31}}, {{Leviticus 19:34|34}}, {{Leviticus 19:36|36}}, {{Leviticus 19:37|37}}). Each use reminded Israel why they must obey God's rules.

*you are not to reap ... Leave them for the poor and the foreigner:* Israel's covenant with God included a social structure that promoted equality and resisted social divisions. Families had to support relatives facing difficulties. Widows and orphans, the poor, and foreigners were part of Israel's extended family ({{Exodus 22:22|Exodus 22:22}}; {{Leviticus 19:10|Leviticus 19:10}}). The poor received special consideration in the offering system and measures ensured they had food to eat ({{Leviticus 5:7-13|5:7–13}}).

A society that does not respect the property of others would quickly collapse. {{Exodus 20:15|Exodus 20:15}}prohibited stealing. Those who deceived or cheated had to present a guilt offering (see {{Leviticus 6:2-7|Leviticus 6:2–7}}).
*profane the name:* This means to blaspheme (speak in a way that dishonors God; study note on Leviticus 18:21).

Day laborers did not own land and were among the poorest in Israel. These workers relied on landowners for their income. A *hired hand* needed to receive his wages promptly to feed his family ({{Deuteronomy 24:15|Deuteronomy 24:15}}). This verse considers withholding their wages as cheating them.
People who could not hear and people who could not see were vulnerable. Others could easily mistreat them. God told the Israelites not to take advantage of them.
In a legal case, judges were not to favor either the poor or the rich. Justice had to come first at all times (see {{Exodus 23:3|Exodus 23:3}}, {{Exodus 23:6|6}}).

*You must not go about spreading slander: *Imagine a merchant who trades in damaging rumors and accusations. This behavior quickly weakens the valued community spirit in Israel (see {{Proverbs 11:13|Proverbs 11:13}}; {{Proverbs 16:28|16:28}}; {{Proverbs 20:19|20:19}}; {{Proverbs 26:20|26:20}}; {{2 Corinthians 12:20|2 Corinthians 12:20}}).

- *your brother in your heart:* The Hebrew term can refer to any fellow Israelite. All of Israel was one family (compare {{1 John 3:15|1 John 3:15}}). 

- *Directly rebuke:* Love does not mean ignoring wrong actions. Correcting someone can help them change.

*love your neighbor as yourself:* This is a key principle in biblical ethics found in both the Old and New Testaments (see {{Matthew 22:39|Matt 22:39}}; {{Mark 12:31|Mark 12:31}}; {{Luke 10:27|Luke 10:27}}; {{Romans 13:8-9|Romans 13:8–9}}; {{Galatians 5:14|Galatians 5:14}}; {{James 2:8|James 2:8}}). It includes loving foreigners ({{Leviticus 19:34|Leviticus 19:34}}; compare {{Luke 10:30-37|Luke 10:30–37}}). In contrast, hate can lead to grudges and violence (see {{1 John 2:10-11|1 John 2:10–11}}; {{1 John 4:20|4:20}}).

*two kinds:* God created a natural order ({{Genesis 1:31|Genesis 1:31}}; see {{Leviticus 18:22|Leviticus 18:22}}). People violate it when they do not honor God's boundaries. The prohibitions against intermixing served as lessons for the Israelites, who were not to intermarry with the Canaanites.

In the biblical world, betrothal (engagement) was viewed as equal to marriage. Having sexual relations with a betrothed woman who was not a slave brought the same punishment as adultery. The punishment was death ({{Deuteronomy 22:22|Deuteronomy 22:22}}; see {{Leviticus 18:20|Leviticus 18:20}}). 

The situation was less clear if the woman was a slave, since she might not be able to refuse. Slaves in Israel had more rights than those in Mesopotamia or Egypt, but they were still not free. They could not punish a slave girl, so the man also went unpunished. Yet, he was guilty in God's eyes and had to sacrifice a ram for his sin.

For the first three years, they should only prune and cultivate a newly planted fruit tree. This helps the tree grow strong. In the fourth year, people considered all of the fruit the "fitrstfruits" and gave the fruit to God (see {{Exodus 23:16|Exodus 23:16}}). People could only eat the fruit in the fifth year.

- *blood:* See study note on Leviticus 7:22–27. 

- Priests could consult the Urim and Thummim ({{Exodus 28:30|Exodus 28:30}}). They could also cast lots to decide cases not addressed in the laws Moses gave ({{Leviticus 16:8|Leviticus 16:8}}). But those who practiced fortune-telling or witchcraft consulted a power other than the Lord. The first commandment prohibited this ({{Exodus 20:3|Exodus 20:3}}).

*do not clip off:* Egyptian wall paintings show that Canaanites trimmed their hair and beards carefully. The Israelites were told not to copy this practice so that they would not be influenced by Canaanite religion and ethics.

*cuts in your bodies:* Cutting oneself was associated with Canaanite mourning practices ({{Leviticus 21:5|Leviticus 21:5}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:1|Deuteronomy 14:1}}). The word translated as "tattoo" might mean painting the body, a practice also associated with paganism.

- *My Sabbaths:* The Hebrew word for “Sabbath” (*shabbath*) comes from a verb meaning “to cease,” suggesting rest from work. 

The Sabbath recalled God's rest on the seventh day after creating the world ({{Genesis 1:31|Genesis 1:31}}; {{Genesis 2:1-3|2:1–3}}). It started at sundown on the sixth day. After the exodus from Egypt, the Sabbath took on covenantal importance ({{Exodus 16:23-25|Exodus 16:23–25}}; {{Exodus 31:13|31:13}}). Only free people, not slaves, had a regular rest day. So the Sabbath symbolized Israel’s freedom from slavery in Egypt (see {{Deuteronomy 5:13-15|Deuteronomy 5:13–15}}). 

- The people were to *have reverence* (literally *fear*) because the sanctuary, like the Sabbath, was holy. They were not to enter it when ceremonially unclean or bring anything unclean into it.

- *mediums:* Compare {{1 Samuel 28:7-25|1 Samuel 28:7–25}}. 

- The Hebrew term for *spiritists* (*yidde‘oni*) comes from a root meaning "to know." It describes people who claim to have secret or occult knowledge and who try to communicate with the dead.
In ancient times, people respected the elderly for their wisdom ({{Job 32:7|Job 32:7}}). Respecting the elderly also shows respect for God.
The Israelites were once foreigners living in Egypt. God commanded them to remember how the Egyptians mistreated them and show love to the foreigners (see {{Deuteronomy 10:19|Deuteronomy 10:19}}).

*dishonest measures:* Merchants sometimes used two sets of weights, one heavy and one light to cheat customers ({{Deuteronomy 25:13-15|Deuteronomy 25:13–15}}). The Bible clearly states that God detested this practice ({{Proverbs 11:1|Proverbs 11:1}}; {{Proverbs 16:11|16:11}}; {{Proverbs 20:10|20:10}}, {{Proverbs 20:23|23}}; {{Micah 6:11|Micah 6:11}}).

*The people of the land are to stone him:* This was the usual method for carrying out the death penalty (see also {{Leviticus 20:27|Leviticus 20:27}}; {{Leviticus 24:14|24:14}}, {{Leviticus 24:16|16}}, {{Leviticus 24:23|23}}; {{Exodus 19:13|Exodus 19:13}}; {{Numbers 15:35-36|Numbers 15:35–36}}; {{Deuteronomy 17:2-7|Deuteronomy 17:2–7}}; {{Joshua 7:25-26|Joshua 7:25–26}}; {{John 8:1-11|John 8:1–11}}).

The Hebrew word for *curses* means "to make light of, treat with contempt." It is traditionally translated as "curse," meaning to call someone a vulgar or profane name. Parental authority was given by God, not chosen by the child (see {{Exodus 20:12|Exodus 20:12}}; {{Deuteronomy 21:18-21|Deuteronomy 21:18–21}}).

Pagan worship influenced ethics, so God has family rules follow those about pagan religious practices. Some laws in this section repeat parts from {{Leviticus 18:6-30|Leviticus 18:6–30}}, which come before the section on proper expressions of holiness ({{Leviticus 19:1-37|19:1–37}}). These issues connect. Proper worship of God leads to good behavior toward others, while improper worship leads to moral violations.
See study note on Leviticus 18:20. See also {{Exodus 20:14|Exodus 20:14}}.
See study note on Leviticus 18:7–8. This rule made it clear that this act was both incest and adultery.

- *a disgrace: *Proper behavior brings honor to individuals and their families. Improper behavior brings shame. 

- Both parties are cut off, but they will punish the man (see {{Leviticus 7:20-21|Leviticus 7:20–21}}; {{Leviticus 5:1|5:1}}; {{Leviticus 18:6|18:6}}).

Being childless brought public shame in society. People considered it a judgment from God (see {{Genesis 30:1-2|Genesis 30:1–2}}; {{Deuteronomy 7:14|Deuteronomy 7:14}}). 

What situation do these verses describe? {{Leviticus 18:14|Leviticus 18:14}}{{Leviticus 18:16|,16}}already discuss sexual relations with an uncle’s wife or sister-in-law. {{Deuteronomy 22:22|Deuteronomy 22:22}}addresses adultery that results in death for both involved. If the woman was a widow without a male heir, the law of levirate marriage could apply ({{Deuteronomy 25:5-6|Deuteronomy 25:5–6}}; see study note on Leviticus 18:16). 

Since those situations do not seem to apply, this law probably refers to marrying an aunt or a sister-in-law after her divorce. John the Baptist apparently used this law to condemn Herod Antipas’s marriage to Herodias (see {{Mark 6:17-29|Mark 6:17–29}}).

The phrase *flowing with milk and honey *appears often in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. It means that there is plenty of food and it easy to get. This contrasts with Egypt, where everything depended on the flooding of the Nile and irrigation ({{Deuteronomy 11:9-12|Deuteronomy 11:9–12}}).

Touching a dead body made a person ceremonially unclean for seven days. A priest needed to be ready to handle holy things at all times. So, he could not touch a dead body, even if it was a relative's. Otherwise, he might be unable to serve when needed. The only exceptions were his closest relatives, as there might be no one else to bury them.

This section, which discusses priestly rules, six times repeats the phrase *I am the Lord who sanctifies* ({{Leviticus 21:15|Leviticus 21:15}}, {{Leviticus 21:23|23}}; {{Leviticus 22:9|22:9}}, {{Leviticus 22:16|16}}, {{Leviticus 22:32|32}}; see also {{Leviticus 21:8|21:8}}). These words emphasize the link between God's holiness and the holiness expected of priests. This extended to all of Israel (see {{Leviticus 8:10|8:10}}; {{Leviticus 11:44-45|11:44–45}}; {{Leviticus 19:2|19:2}}). The text specifically addresses priests in {{Leviticus 21:1-22:16|21:1–22:16}}, while including both clergy and common people in {{Leviticus 22:17-33|22:17–33}}.

- *make bald spots … shave off:* The laws warned priests not to shave or trim their hair in certain ways (see study notes on Leviticus 10:6; 19:27). 

- * make cuts in their bodies:* They were also not to cut their bodies (see study note on Leviticus 19:28). Cutting the body was a practice of pagan peoples. Defects disqualified most animals as offerings ({{Leviticus 22:19-25|Leviticus 22:19–25}}). A defect also disqualified a priest from serving (see {{Leviticus 21:17-23|21:17–23}}). 

For example, a eunuch (a man unable to reproduce) could not serve as a priest because he was not a suitable representative of the people ({{Deuteronomy 23:1|Deuteronomy 23:1}}). But his priestly family line allowed him to eat his priestly share (see {{Leviticus 21:22|Leviticus 21:22}}). On the other hand, if a priest became unclean, he could not serve in ministry or eat the priest’s share until he was clean again ({{Leviticus 22:2-8|22:2–8}}).
A priest must never dishonor God by treating his name as unholy.

The priest had to set a high standard of conduct for Israel in worship. This applied to his personal life and family leadership. He could not have any connections to pagan practices (for example, prostitution, {{Leviticus 21:9|Leviticus 21:9}}). His family also had to be above question, so divorce was not allowed. Early church leaders followed similar standards ({{1 Timothy 3:1-13|1 Timothy 3:1–13}}).

- The rules for common priests were more strict than for the high priest, who represented all of Israel, including other priests ({{Leviticus 21:1-4|Leviticus 21:1–4}}). 

- The priest must always keep his hair neat and not tear his clothing in mourning. This ensured he was always ready to serve. While a common priest could marry a widow, the high priest could only marry a virgin. This ensured that future high priests and common priests from that union would have a clear lineage ({{Leviticus 21:15|Leviticus 21:15}}).

*He may eat:* If a descendant of Aaron had a mutilation or defect, he could not serve as a priest to represent the people (see {{Leviticus 21:18-20|Leviticus 21:18–20}}). But his priestly family line still counted. He was allowed to eat the priest’s share of the offerings (see {{Leviticus 2:3|2:3}}, {{Leviticus 2:10|10}}; {{Leviticus 6:17-18|6:17–18}}).

They considered the priest's portions of the sacred offerings "most holy" (see {{Leviticus 2:3|Leviticus 2:3}}). He had to avoid contact with anything ceremonially unclean ({{Leviticus 11:1-15:33|11:1–15:33}}). So, any descendant of Aaron who was unclean could not eat this food.

In Leviticus, the Hebrew word *sherets* always refers to an unclean small animal that swarms on land or in water ({{Leviticus 5:2|Leviticus 5:2}}; {{Leviticus 11:10|11:10}}, {{Leviticus 11:20-21|20–21}}, {{Leviticus 11:23|23}}, {{Leviticus 11:29|29}}, {{Leviticus 11:31|31}}, {{Leviticus 11:41-44|41–44}}).

*die because they profane it *(see {{Leviticus 10:1-3|Leviticus 10:1–3}}): The temptation to make improper offerings continued throughout Israel's history until after the exile in Babylon ({{Malachi 1:6-9|Malachi 1:6–9}}).
The only male outside the priest's family who could eat the priest's share was the priest's slave. Without this provision, the slave would have no other food.

Like the rules for the guilt offering, a common person who accidentally ate the priestly portion had to repay 120 percent (see {{Leviticus 5:14-16|Leviticus 5:14–16}}). Yet, they did not need to offer a ram in this case.
An Israelite who ate the “most holy” food meant only for priests as if it were ordinary food would profane it (treat it as unholy).
People could choose to present *a gift* instead of *a burnt offering* (see {{Leviticus 1:3|1:3}}).

A peace offering could be given in different ways: 

- as a thanksgiving offering,

- an offering to fulfill a vow, or

- as a voluntary offering (see {{Leviticus 3:1-17|Leviticus 3:1–17}}).

The rules for voluntary offerings were less strict, allowing the use of a deformed animal. But fulfilling a vow still required an animal that was not injured or sick. God would not accept a sacrifice that a person could not eat or that was not a whole animal.
Keeping a newborn animal with its mother for seven days helped determine the animal's health (see {{Exodus 22:30|Exodus 22:30}}).

*on the same day:* There are several possible explanations for this command, although none is certain: 

- Senseless slaughtering would leave nothing of the herd;

- it would be cruel to slaughter the young and the mother at the same time; or

- it would resemble pagan worship rites, where people cooked the newborn animal in the milk of its slain mother (see {{Exodus 23:19|Exodus 23:19}}).

God wanted his people to remember that all good things come from him. God gave them many ways to remember this.

Lamps that never burnt out and holy bread on the gold table reminded them. So did the smell of incense burning in the holy tent.

The feasts the Israelites celebrated also reminded them. The Sabbath day reminded them that God provided the rest they needed.

Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread reminded them of when God rescued them. He rescued them when they were slaves in Egypt.

Offering the first share of crops would remind them that God provided their food when they entered Canaan. The Feast of Weeks also reminded them of this. Later the Feast of Weeks was called Pentecost.

The Feast of Trumpets invited the Israelites to rest and to turn away from sin. The day when sin was paid for was also called the Day of Atonement. It reminded them that God forgave their sins.

The Feast of Booths would remind them how God took care of them when they left Egypt.
These appointed festivals included times for eating, resting, and fasting. For more details, see {{Numbers 28:1-29:40|Numbers 28–29}}.

- *Passover* started at sundown on the fourteenth day of the first month, as the new day began (see study note on Leviticus 11:24–25). *The Passover* feast included a roast lamb, bitter salad greens, and bread without yeast ({{Exodus 12:8|Exodus 12:8}}). These foods represented Israel’s freedom from Egyptian slavery.

- The first month marked the start of the Jewish calendar as late as {{Ezra 6:19|Ezra 6:19}}. The month’s earliest name was *Abib* (which means “spring, fresh grain”; {{Exodus 13:4|Exodus 13:4}}; {{Exodus 23:15|23:15}}; {{Exodus 34:18|34:18}}; {{Deuteronomy 16:1|Deuteronomy 16:1}}). The name *Nisan* partly replaced *Abib *after the exile of Israel to Babylon ({{Nehemiah 2:1|Nehemiah 2:1}}; {{Esther 3:7|Esther 3:7}}).

*Passover … Unleavened Bread:* These feasts began on the evening before the exodus from Egypt (see {{Exodus 12:1-28|Exodus 12:1–28}}). 

Israel had three major festivals:

- The Feast of Unleavened Bread, which begins the day after Passover ({{Deuteronomy 16:16|Deuteronomy 16:16}})

- The Festival of Weeks ({{Leviticus 23:15-21|Leviticus 23:15–21}})

- The Festival of Tabernacles ({{Leviticus 23:34-43|23:34–43}})

After Passover came *the Feast of Unleavened Bread*. During this time, Israel ate bread made without yeast. This bread reminded them of their slavery in Egypt and the quickness of their departure from Egypt (see study note on Leviticus 2:11, {{Deuteronomy 16:3|Deuteronomy 16:3}}).

The burned part of each sacrifice stood for the whole offering, and the tithe symbolized that all of a person's money belonged to God. In a similar way, the first portions of each harvest, or firstfruits, represented the entire harvest and even the land itself as belonging to God ({{Leviticus 25:23|Leviticus 25:23}}). 

During the barley harvest, people offered the first portions as part of the Feast of Unleavened Bread ({{Leviticus 23:6|Leviticus 23:6}}, {{Leviticus 23:10-12|10–12}}). They offered the first portions of the wheat harvest during "the Feast of Weeks" ({{Leviticus 23:15-21|23:15–21}}; {{Exodus 34:22|Exodus 34:22}}). These gifts to God acknowledged God's earlier gifts to Israel (see {{Leviticus 2:1|Leviticus 2:1}}). The entire offering of firstfruits became the property and food of God's representatives, the priests (see {{Leviticus 2:14-16|2:14–16}}).
The phrase *wave it* symbolizes offering the grain to the Lord (see study note on Leviticus 7:34).
The Israelites could not eat from the harvest that day until they acknowledged God's gift by making the appropriate offering.

Israel was to start counting seven full weeks from the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread. The fiftieth day marked the start of the Feast of Weeks (harvest). The New Testament calls this "Pentecost," from the Greek word for "fifty." 

During this festival, people offered the first portions of the wheat harvest. Each person also had to take three quarts of fine flour and bake two loaves of yeast bread. They then presented these offerings to the priest at the sanctuary. See also study note on Exodus 23:16.
The *drink offerings* probably contained two quarts of wine (see {{Exodus 29:40|Exodus 29:40}}; {{Numbers 15:5|Numbers 15:5}}, {{Numbers 15:10|10}}).

*On the first day of the seventh month:* the Israelite calendar divided into two half-years. The first half-year began with the first month, called *Nisan* (Babylonian name) or *Abib* (the older agricultural name). The second half-year began with the seventh month, known as *Tishri* on the modern Jewish calendar. This holiday celebration marked the start of the second half-year.

The Day of Atonement was the most serious and holy day in the Israelite calendar and the only day of fasting (chapter {{Leviticus 16:1-34|Leviticus 16}}). The high priest atoned for the people's collective sin. This gave the theological basis (the main teaching and reason) for the greater atonement made by Jesus Christ ({{Hebrews 9:11-12|Hebrews 9:11–12}}).
*cut off … destroy:* See study note on Leviticus 7:20–21; compare with {{Exodus 31:14|Exodus 31:14}}, {{Exodus 31:15|15}}; {{Exodus 35:2|35:2}}.

During *the Feast of Tabernacles*, the Israelites lived in temporary shelters for seven days. This celebrated the time they spent in tents during their wilderness wanderings. It also reminded them of God's faithfulness during that period. For a list of sacrifices to be offered each day, see {{Numbers 29:12-34|Numbers 29:12–34}}.

*after you have gathered the produce:* The Feast of Tabernacles was also called the Feast of Ingathering because people gathered all the fruit and vegetables that were not yet harvested ({{Exodus 34:22|Exodus 34:22}}).

God did not want the Israelites to ever forget his great acts of redemption for them. They needed to teach each new generation about what God had done ({{Deuteronomy 4:9|Deuteronomy 4:9}}; {{Deuteronomy 11:19|11:19}}). Their identity and understanding of themselves and God depended on this knowledge. See {{Deuteronomy 6:20-24|Deuteronomy 6:20–24}}; {{Deuteronomy 26:5-9|26:5–9}}; {{Joshua 24:2-13|Joshua 24:2–13}}; {{Psalm 136:1-26|Psalm 136}}.

Traditionally called the “shewbread” in the King James Version, this bread was made of twelve flat loaves. It is also called the "Bread of the Presence." Every Sabbath, the loaves were placed on the table in the Holy Place (see {{Exodus 25:30|Exodus 25:30}} and {{Exodus 25:23-30|Exodus 25:23–30}}). This bread was part of the priest's share of the offerings. David and his men ate this bread while escaping from King Saul (see {{1 Samuel 21:1-6|1 Samuel 21:1–6}} and {{Matthew 12:1-8|Matthew 12:1–8}}).
The priests burned a portion of this bread as an offering (see {{Leviticus 2:2|2:2}}). So they made the bread without yeast ("unleavened"; see {{Leviticus 2:11|2:11}}).

The Israelites were to be held responsible for the wrong things that they did. This was also true for everyone who lived in their community. It included when they sinned against God by speaking evil things against his name. It also included harm they caused to others.

They were to be punished according to the hurt they had caused other people. This was different from the violent example of Lamech in Genesis 4:23–24. Lamech killed people who hurt him. He boasted about hurting people 77 times more than they had hurt him.

Later, Jesus taught his followers about forgiving people who hurt them.

A large group of non-Israelites, including other Semitic people and Egyptians, left Egypt with the Israelites ({{Exodus 12:38|Exodus 12:38}}). Among them was a man with an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father. A fight broke out between this man and a full-blooded Israelite. the man who was half-Egyptian verbally cursed the Israelite, using the name of God in a disrespectful manner.

- *blasphemed … with a curse:* In biblical times, a name was more than a title. It represented a person's character, reputation, and origin. God is holy, and he required the Israelites to treat him as holy in all aspects of life (see {{Leviticus 10:3|Leviticus 10:3}}). God's instructed them to show respect for God's name ({{Exodus 20:7|Exodus 20:7}}). Using God's name in a curse showed a sinful attitude toward God ({{Leviticus 24:15|Leviticus 24:15}}). It was punishable by death ({{Leviticus 24:13-16|24:13–16}}). 

The Hebrew text in this passage uses two different words for "curse." One refers to a formal type of curse, while the other means a blasphemous or irreverent expression. These terms are used together in {{Leviticus 24:15-16|24:15–16}} to show the seriousness of the offense.

- *the Name:* The Hebrew text referes only to "the Name." This wording shows care and respect for God's name.

Those who heard someone curse against God had to *lay their hands on his head*. This act showed their innocence by symbolically transferring the guilt (see {{Leviticus 16:21|Leviticus 16:21}}). It also showed their willingness to take responsibility for the person's death. A single witness was not enough to sentence someone to death (see {{Numbers 35:30|Numbers 35:30}}; {{Deuteronomy 17:2-7|Deuteronomy 17:2–7}}; {{Matthew 18:16|Matthew 18:16}}; {{2 Corinthians 13:1|2 Corinthians 13:1}}; {{1 Timothy 5:19|1 Timothy 5:19}}; {{Hebrews 10:28|Hebrews 10:28}}).

Because human life was made in the image of God ({{Genesis 1:26|Genesis 1:26}}, {{Genesis 1:27|27}}), murder was seen as an attack against God himself. It carried the same penalty as speaking blasphemy against God ({{Genesis 9:6|Genesis 9:6}}). For a similar law and its details, see {{Exodus 21:12-14|Exodus 21:12–14}}.

*eye for eye:* This legal principle is often called *lex talionis* (which means “law of retaliation”). This means the punishment should match the crime. When an injured person sought revenge for their family member, excessive revenge often occurred instead of proper justice (see {{Numbers 35:19-21|Numbers 35:19–21}}). This led to even more retaliation, creating a cycle of increasing violence. *Lex talionis* helped regulate how to prosecute crimes (see also {{Leviticus 6:2-7|Leviticus 6:2–7}}; compare {{Exodus 21:24|Exodus 21:24}}; {{Leviticus 24:20|Leviticus 24:20}}; {{Deuteronomy 19:21|Deuteronomy 19:21}}; {{Matthew 5:28-39|Matthew 5:28–39}}).
Foreigners were not citizens, but they were human beings who deserved equal justice under the law (see {{Leviticus 16:29|Leviticus 16:29}}, {{Leviticus 16:31|31}}).

The people groups around the Israelites didn’t honour a Sabbath day of rest. Nor did they practice a sabbath year or a Year of Jubilee. These practices set the Israelites apart. They showed that everything belonged to God. The work the people did belonged to him. So did the weeks and years that they lived. The land where God allowed them to live also belonged to him.

The sabbath year happened every seventh year when the Israelites stopped farming. This allowed the land to rest just like people rested on the Sabbath day. It was one way to be faithful rulers of the land God gave them. It also showed that the Israelites trusted God to provide food for them.

The Year of Jubilee happened every fifty years. It was another year when the land rested instead of being farmed. It stopped any changes people made about who owned certain land. The land was returned to the tribes and families God had first given it to. The Israelites were set free from debts of money they owed to others. The Year of Jubilee also stopped any Israelites from working as servants for other Israelites. This reminded the Israelites that they were servants only of God. Because they belonged to God, they weren’t to be bought and sold as slaves.

Just as seven days made a week ending in a Sabbath day, every seven years ended with a Sabbath year. After seven Sabbath years, or 49 years, came a special year called the Year of Jubilee. Like so many holy days, these times were meant for reflecting on Israel's shared identity and their relationship with God. 

Every Israelite, both free and servant, had a place in God’s kingdom. So, those bound in servitude were set free during the Year of Jubilee ({{Leviticus 25:39-43|Leviticus 25:39–43}}). To reduce poverty and protect families, land sales were limited to fifty years. After that, the land returned to the original owner's family or clan. 

The land belonged to God, and the Israelites were only "residents" ({{Leviticus 25:23|25:23}}). But it is unlikely that they actually used these laws. The best land ended up belonging to wealthy landowners ({{Isaiah 5:8-10|Isaiah 5:8–10}}; compare {{Amos 5:11|Amos 5:11}}).

*during the Sabbath year, *people did not formally farm or harvest the land. Landowners could gather what naturally grew for their daily household needs. They left any uneaten food for the poor and foreigners ({{Exodus 23:10-11|Exodus 23:10–11}}). What remained provided food for both wild and domestic animals. See also {{Exodus 21:2|Exodus 21:2}}; {{Deuteronomy 15:1-11|Deuteronomy 15:1–11}}.

*there shall be a Sabbath of complete rest for the land: *The idea of the *Sabbath* is that God rested, so people must rest also (see study note on Leviticus 19:30). This idea also applies to the land.

- The Year of Jubilee occurred every fiftieth year, releasing people from obligations and slavery. This year was also a Sabbath year, meaning no farming took place. 

Some scholars believe the forty-ninth year was both a Sabbath (seventh) and Jubilee (fiftieth) year. Counting fifty years would place the Year of Jubilee right after the seventh Sabbath year, leading to two years without harvests. 

- During each Year of Jubilee, the land returned to the original clan or tribe that received it under Joshua ({{Joshua 13:1-21:45|Joshua 13–21}}). 

Land had two purposes: 

- It provided an economic foundation for living. 

- It connected the landowner to ancestors. Through them it connected the land distribution under Joshua and the covenant with Moses. 

Returning the land intended to prevent powerful land monopolies that could exclude the poor.

- *proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants:* See {{Leviticus 25:39-43|Leviticus 25:39–43}}, {{Leviticus 25:47-55|47–55}}. 

- *return to his property and to his clan: *If the original landowner had died, his heirs received the land.
The rules for the Sabbath year also applied to the Year of Jubilee.

*the number of years:* The law did not allow permanent sale of the land. It belonged to God, and Israel was simply allowed to use it ({{Leviticus 25:23|Leviticus 25:23}}). If the owner had to give up the land because of financial problems, he could lease it for up to forty-nine years, until the next Jubilee. The price depended on the lease length. At the end of that period, the land returned to the original owner's family.

*it is Mine:* Israel did not own the land in an absolute way. Their right to live there depended on the covenant, because God himself gave them the land ({{Deuteronomy 1:8|Deuteronomy 1:8}}, {{Deuteronomy 1:39|39}}). From this idea of God’s ownership comes the call to care for the land as stewards and to share material resources with others.

The Hebrew word *ga’al* means "to restore something to its original or proper state." The noun form of this Hebrew root (*go’el*) refers to a close relative who will fix what is wrong. 

This relative's duties included: 

- redeeming a kinsman's property to keep it in the family (see {{Ruth 4:1-4|Ruth 4:1–4}}; {{Jeremiah 32:6-15|Jeremiah 32:6–15}});

- searching for the kinsman's murderer and bringing him to justice ({{Numbers 35:19|Numbers 35:19}}); and

- marrying his brother's widow to produce a male heir for the estate of the dead brother ({{Deuteronomy 25:5-10|Deuteronomy 25:5–10}}; see {{Genesis 38:6-30|Genesis 38:6–30}}; {{Ruth 4:9-10|Ruth 4:9–10}}).

A house in a village without walls was treated the same as land. The family could buy it back. If they did not, it returned to the seller’s family in the Year of Jubilee.

But a house inside a walled town was different. No farmland or pasture was included in the sale of such a house. A house could even be built on the town wall without touching the ground ({{Joshua 2:15|Josh 2:15}}). For this reason, the land was not part of the property.

Such a house could not be bought back unless the new owner chose to sell it. It also did not return to the original family in the Year of Jubilee.

The tribe of Levi did not inherit land like other tribes. As the priestly tribe, they lived throughout the land ({{Deuteronomy 18:1|Deuteronomy 18:1}}; see {{Genesis 49:5-7|Genesis 49:5–7}}; {{Numbers 35:1-8|Numbers 35:1–8}}; {{Joshua 21:1-42|Josh 21:1–42}}). The Levites could only inherit specific cities and the surrounding pasturelands ({{Numbers 35:2|Numbers 35:2}}). 

The Levites were an exception to land ownership rules. They carefully protected their small holdings. They could redeem their houses even in walled cities. They could not sell the pasturelands outside their towns.

*destitute:* Poor Israelites first asked their family for help (see study note on Leviticus 25:25). Second, they depended on the community. God commanded the people to help the poor instead of taking advantage of them.

The purpose of a loan was to help a poor person financially recover, not to profit from their vulnerability. Israelites could not charge interest on loans to Israelites. But Israelites could charge interest on loans to foreigners ({{Deuteronomy 23:19-20|Deuteronomy 23:19–20}}).

The mention of *the land of Egypt* reminded the Israelites that they were once slaves. They needed to help the poor among them because of God's covenant with them. Compare {{Exodus 20:2|Exodus 20:2}} and {{Deuteronomy 5:6|Deuteronomy 5:6}}, where God begins his covenant with them.

- The terms *hired worker or temporary resident* are used together, showing they were similar in Israel’s social and economic life. Both described day laborers who had no land of their own and depended on landowners for work (see {{Matthew 20:1-16|Matthew 20:1–16}}; also see study note on Leviticus 19:13). 

- *Jubilee:* See study note on Leviticus 25:8–17.
The same Hebrew word means both *servants* and *slaves*. The Israelites were God's servants, so they could not be slaves to other people. They could only serve temporarily to pay off a debt.

God created human beings in his image ({{Genesis 1:26|Genesis 1:26}}, {{Genesis 1:27|27}}; {{Proverbs 14:31|Proverbs 14:31}}; {{Proverbs 17:5|17:5}}). Fellow Israelites were in a covenant with God. So, even bondservants must receive respect. God's law includes many rules to protect them (see {{Exodus 21:20|Exodus 21:20}}, {{Exodus 21:26-27|26–27}}). Everyone must treat others in a way that shows reverence for God (see {{Proverbs 14:31|Proverbs 14:31}}; {{Proverbs 17:5|17:5}}; {{James 2:14-16|James 2:14–16}}; {{James 3:9-10|3:9–10}}).

In Mesopotamia and Egypt, people treated slaves like property. They had no rights or protection. Among the Israelites, people could purchase non-Israelites as slaves. Yet God commanded that they be treated well and not abused. Sometimes a slave was even adopted into a childless family ({{Genesis 15:2-4|Genesis 15:2–4}}). 

Slavery continued in New Testament times. However, the Old Testament taught that all people share a common beginning because God created humankind. This belief laid the foundation for the later rejection of slavery.

Slavery began after the first humans sinned. This was the start of power-based relationships replacing those of friendship and communication (see {{Genesis 3:16|Genesis 3:16}}). 

In the New Testament, Christians promote fellowship and communication by calling themselves “a servant of Christ Jesus"({{Romans 1:1|Romans 1:1}}; {{Colossians 4:12|Colossians 4:12}}; {{2 Peter 1:1|2 Peter 1:1}}). In Paul's teachings on "the body of Christ" ({{1 Corinthians 12:27|1 Corinthians 12:27}}; {{Ephesians 4:12|Ephesians 4:12}}), all Christians share a common identity ({{Galatians 3:28|Galatians 3:28}}; {{Colossians 3:11|Colossians 3:11}}; {{Philemon 16|Philemon 1:16}}).

An Israelite who sold himself or a family member to a foreigner in Israel could buy himself or the family member back. If he lacked the resources to do so, he remained a slave in the seventh year. He had to wait for release in the Year of Jubilee (compare {{Exodus 21:2|Exodus 21:2}}). While serving the foreigner, they must treat the Israelite slave as a hired servant, not as a slave (see {{Leviticus 25:53|Leviticus 25:53}}). The people of Israel belonged to God. No one could sell them as permanent slaves to anyone else.

- God instructed Israel not to make idols or carved images to worship (see {{Exodus 20:4-6|Exodus 20:4–6}}). Creating an image to worship would would insult God. It limited God to time and space and replaced the living God with a lifeless object. 

- Early in Israel's history, people set up stones as memorials for various events ({{Genesis 28:18|Genesis 28:18}}; {{Exodus 24:4|Exodus 24:4}}). Yet, pillars and sculpted stones had connections to pagan worship ({{2 Kings 3:2|2 Kings 3:2}}; {{2 Kings 10:26|10:26}}, {{2 Kings 10:27|27}}). This was especially true when these stones held the carved image of a god. God clearly allowed for some sculptures (for example, {{1 Kings 7:25|1 Kings 7:25}}). The focus here is on objects that the people would worship, thus making them into idols.

This list of covenant blessings and covenant curses is like the list in Deuteronomy chapters 28 to 30. It described what would happen if the people were faithful to the Mount Sinai covenant. It also described what would happen if they weren’t faithful.

Being faithful to the covenant would lead to wonderful blessings. Life for the Israelites would be like life in the Garden of Eden in many ways. The Israelites would have everything they needed in the land that God had given them. The ground would produce crops as they farmed. They would have plenty to eat and would have many children. They would have peace and live in safety. God’s presence would be with them.

Not being faithful to the covenant would lead to terrible curses. The ground wouldn’t produce crops for them. They would be attacked by enemies and by animals. They would have many diseases and their children would be killed. They would lose the land God had given them. God himself would become their enemy. These things would happen if the Israelites didn’t let the land rest during sabbath years. They would happen if the people didn’t worship only God. They would happen to help the people realise that they had sinned.

But God always remained faithful to his people even when they sinned. They could turn away from their sin and repent. Then God would forgive them and once again give them the covenant blessings.

Treaties and covenants had conditions. Israel's blessings depended on the people's obedience to God's terms, to whom they had sworn obedience ({{Exodus 24:7|Exodus 24:7}}; {{Joshua 24:21-22|Joshua 24:21–22}}). But the covenant itself was unchangeable ({{Leviticus 26:44-45|Leviticus 26:44–45}}; see {{Romans 11:29|Romans 11:29}}). Israel could not cancel it. The people had two choices: obedience, which brought blessings; or rebellion, which brought curses.

These blessings and curses are similar to a key part of ancient Near Eastern treaties between a suzerain (a powerful king) and a vassal (a lesser king). In these treaties, the suzerain king promised to protect the vassal king and his land. In return, the vassal swore loyalty to the suzerain. 

Blessings and curses followed, with curses usually being longer (compare {{Leviticus 26:3-13|Leviticus 26:3–13}} with {{Leviticus 26:14-39|26:14–39}}; see also {{Deuteronomy 27:15-28:68|Deuteronomy 27:15–28:68}}). These treaties often called upon gods as witnesses and enforcers. Yet, in God's covenant with Israel, God was one of the treaty parties, with Israel as the other. Since God could not swear by anyone greater, he swore by himself (see {{Hebrews 6:13|Hebrews 6:13}}; {{Genesis 22:16|Genesis 22:16}}).
When Israel returned from captivity, God promised such a great harvest that it would last until the time of planting the next crops (see {{Amos 9:13|Amos 9:13}}; {{Joel 3:18|Joel 3:18}}).
Success in war would come from obeying God's commands (compare {{Leviticus 26:17|Leviticus 26:17}}, {{Leviticus 26:36-37|36–37}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:6|Deuteronomy 28:6}}, {{Deuteronomy 28:19|19}}).

*establish My covenant:* The fulfillment is in the "rest" mentioned in Hebrews ({{Hebrews 3:11-4:11|Hebrews 3:11–4:11}}). The promised land was meant to provide security and prosperity, a state of "rest," to the Israelites ({{Exodus 33:14|Exodus 33:14}}; {{Deuteronomy 12:10|Deuteronomy 12:10}}; {{Deuteronomy 25:19|25:19}}; {{Joshua 1:13|Joshua 1:13}}, {{Joshua 1:15|15}}). Israel entered the promised land. But their rebellion prevented them from experiencing the covenant being fulfilled.
*your God … My people:* The covenant bound the two groups to one another, making each belong to the other.
*the bars of your yoke:* A yoke is a wooden frame that fits over a slave's shoulders and neck. It is used to carry heavy items like water pails. Compare with {{Romans 6:16-22|Romans 6:16–22}}.

God punishes his people to change their behavior and restore their relationship with him. He acts like a perfectly righteous and loving parent would with a disobedient child. The punishments, meant to stop rebellious behavior, gradually increase. This gives Israel a chance to repent at any time ({{Leviticus 26:18-28|Leviticus 26:18–28}}). Even when Israel faced exile from the land in 722 and 586 BC, God was working to restore them (see, for example, {{Isaiah 40:1-66:24|Isaiah 40–66}}; {{Jeremiah 29:10|Jeremiah 29:10}}; {{Amos 9:11-15|Amos 9:11–15}}).
*sevenfold:* This phrase means many times (see also {{Leviticus 26:21|Leviticus 26:21}}, {{Leviticus 26:24|24}}, {{Leviticus 26:28|28}}; {{Genesis 4:15|Genesis 4:15}}).
If God does not send rain, the ground will become hard and unproductive.

Starvation would become so severe in the land that when a child died of hunger, the family might eat the child’s body. This was a practice seen among pagan nations ({{Deuteronomy 28:53-57|Deuteronomy 28:53–57}}; see {{2 Kings 6:24-31|2 Kings 6:24–31}}; {{Lamentations 2:20|Lamentations 2:20}}; compare {{2 Kings 3:27|2 Kings 3:27}}).

- These pagan shrines mentioned here were the well-known *high places* built on hilltops (see {{2 Kings 18:4|2 Kings 18:4}}). These shrines mixed elements from pre-Israelite religions into Israel's worship. They competed with the temple for religious authority. 

- *incense altars* (Hebrew *khamman*): They used some of these altars in the worship of Baal ({{2 Chronicles 34:4|2 Chronicles 34:4}}).

With the people gone into captivity in a foreign land, there would be no one to work the land. It would at last have the “rest” of lying unworked that the people had denied it (see {{Leviticus 25:1-7|Leviticus 25:1–7}}).
Disastrous defeat and captivity later came upon both Israel and Judah (see study notes on Leviticus 18:28; 26:14–39).

The chapter ends with a hopeful message: Even after Israel broke the covenant and faced judgment, reconciliation and restoration were still possible if the people confessed and repented (see study note on Leviticus 4:20). God’s grace remained. God did not want to destroy his people; he would restore them if they humbled themselves and repented (see also {{2 Chronicles 7:14|2 Chronicles 7:14}}).

Physical circumcision of males was the mark of God's covenant with Israel ({{Genesis 17:9-14|Genesis 17:9–14}}; {{Exodus 4:25-26|Exodus 4:25–26}}). *Uncircumcised hearts *are stubborn hearts that do not love God. The people show this through continual disobedience. God promised to "circumcise" Israel's *uncircumcised hearts *so the people could love Him (see also {{Deuteronomy 10:16|Deuteronomy 10:16}}; {{Deuteronomy 30:6|30:6}}; {{Jeremiah 4:4|Jeremiah 4:4}}; {{Ezekiel 36:25-27|Ezekiel 36:25–27}}).

God had begun his covenant with Abraham (then called Abram, {{Genesis 15:18|Genesis 15:18}}). God continued it with Isaac and Jacob ({{Genesis 17:19|Genesis 17:19}}; {{Exodus 2:24|Exodus 2:24}}). Jacob’s twelve sons became the ancestors of Israel’s twelve tribes. Israel’s freedom from Egypt and settlement in Canaan had its basis in God’s promises to their ancestors, not on the Israelites’ own virtues ({{Deuteronomy 9:4-5|Deuteronomy 9:4–5}}).

God never lies or breaks his promises. The Israelites were to be like him in this way. If they made a promise, they were to keep it.

It was common for Israelites to promise to give God something they cared about. This could be another person, an animal, their house or part of their land. God considered these gifts to be holy.

Sometimes people changed their mind about what they had given to God. When this happened they had to buy back what they had given. This showed that they were still honouring God and keeping their promise.

Some things that the Israelites had they weren’t to use for themselves. This was true about the first male animal born to livestock. It was true about a tenth of all crops and fruit. It was also true about every tenth animal of livestock. These things were only to be used to serve God. This is what it meant that they belonged to the Lord.

The people gave all of these things to God by taking them to the priests. In this way, God provided for the Levites.

This chapter concludes the book by discussing different types of vows. It ends with a rule for redeeming one's tithes (see also chapter {{Leviticus 25:1-55|Leviticus 25}}). At certain times, such as emergencies, a person might vow something to God in exchange for answered prayers (see {{Jonah 2:9|Jonah 2:9}}). After God answered the prayer, the person might want to ignore the vow. Scripture requires that people vow carefully and then fulfill them (see {{Leviticus 5:4|Leviticus 5:4}}; {{Ecclesiastes 5:4-6|Ecclesiastes 5:4–6}}). Jesus taught that people should not make oaths often or carelessly ({{Matthew 5:33-37|Matthew 5:33–37}}; {{Matthew 23:16-22|23:16–22}}).

The vow to become a Nazirite is also called *a special vow* ({{Numbers 6:2|Numbers 6:2}}). Yet, the vow mentioned here was probably a promise made to God when asking for a specific answer to prayer (see {{Genesis 28:20-22|Genesis 28:20–22}}). During that time, some pagan religions sacrificed infants to their gods, but God prohibited this practice ({{Leviticus 18:21|Leviticus 18:21}}; {{Leviticus 20:2-5|20:2–5}}; compare {{Genesis 22:12-13|Genesis 22:12–13}}). 

Therefore, to *make special vow to the Lord* meant providing service, not sacrificing a life. Whether an individual made this vow or by someone on their behalf, it required payment to the sanctuary, probably for the person's expenses during their service. See also {{Numbers 6:1-21|Numbers 6:1–21}}; {{Judges 13:5|Judges 13:5}}, {{Judges 13:7|7}}; {{1 Samuel 1:11|1 Samuel 1:11}}; {{Amos 2:11-12|Amos 2:11–12}}; {{Acts 18:18|Acts 18:18}}.

- This section shows how people were ranked socially in ancient Near Eastern cultures. An adult working man had the highest rank, followed by an adult working woman. A boy ranked higher than a girl, and both ranked higher than toddlers. Senior citizens, who were past their prime working age, ranked similarly to boys and girls. 

- The amount of *fifty shekels* was about 570 grams (20 ounces) of silver, which was a lot (see study note on Leviticus 5:15). Comparisons with other writings from that time show that the biblical shekel value was very high and unaffordable for most people.

Like the offering system (see {{Leviticus 5:7-13|Leviticus 5:7–13}}), God’s law made special allowance for a poor person who wanted to contribute to the sanctuary. In these cases, the priest decided the amount of silver to include with the pledge.
Once someone promised an acceptable animal and the priest at the sanctuary accepted it for God, the animal became holy and belonged to God.

An unclean animal, not suitable for food or sacrifice, could be bought back by the worshiper for its assessed value plus 20 percent. This rule likely aimed to preserve the sanctity of vows and reduce careless dedications. For the 20 percent additional charge on property, see {{Leviticus 27:15|Leviticus 27:15}}, {{Leviticus 27:19|19}}, {{Leviticus 27:31|31}}.

- The Hebrew term translated as *consecrates* is emphatic and means "declares holy." 

- This rule applies only to a house in a walled town. Other houses, whether in unwalled villages or on open land, returned to the owner in the Year of Jubilee ({{Leviticus 25:29-31|Leviticus 25:29–31}}). If the owner wanted to redeem it, he had to pay an extra 20 percent. If he did not redeem the house in the first year, it became the property of the sanctuary and priests. They could use it as they wished.

The cost to consecrate a field depended on the years left until the next *Year of Jubilee* (see {{Leviticus 25:24-28|Leviticus 25:24–28}}). If not redeemed, the property became the priests' to use as they wanted. Redeeming a field cost 120 percent of its valuation (see {{Leviticus 27:11-13|27:11–13}}). If a landowner consecrated his field without redeeming it, it did not return to his family in *the Year of Jubilee*.

- *Year of Jubilee:* See {{Leviticus 25:8-55|Leviticus 25:8–55}}. 

- *devoted to the LORD:* When someone made a vow to devote something to the Lord, that thing became holy. It could not be bought back or exchanged.
Each of the *gerahs* weighed about 0.02 ounces or 0.6 grams.

*no one may consecrate:* Every firstborn male, whether human or animal, already belonged to God ({{Exodus 13:2|Exodus 13:2}}; {{Exodus 34:19-20|34:19–20}}). Thus, consecrating a firstborn is unnecessary. Priests use the firstborn of animals suitable for food or sacrifice (ceremonially clean animals). You can redeem the firstborn of a ceremonially unclean animal, like a donkey, for 20 percent more than its value. Firstborn humans had to be redeemed ({{Exodus 13:11-13|Exodus 13:11–13}}).
*sets apart* (Hebrew *kherem*): This act of devotion could not be undone. The person, animal, or property devoted in this way became dedicated to the service of the sanctuary as the priest defined.

*set apart for destruction* (Hebrew *kherem*): This is the same Hebrew word used in the previous verse. The context here is the Israelite war to conquer Canaan. God *set apart for destruction* cities, animals, and people considered holy to other gods.

One-tenth of the harvest (called the "tithe") belonged to the Lord ({{Deuteronomy 14:22-26|Deuteronomy 14:22–26}}; compare {{Leviticus 23:10-14|Leviticus 23:10–14}}). The tribe of Levi, which included priests and Levites, did not receive tribal lands. Instead, they received one-tenth of all produce from landowners ({{Numbers 18:21-29|Numbers 18:21–29}}). They set aside this tithe each year ({{Deuteronomy 14:22|Deuteronomy 14:22}}). They took it to the sanctuary, where they ate part of it in a ceremony meal ({{Deuteronomy 14:23-26|Deuteronomy 14:23–26}}). 

Every third year, they gave a second tithe locally to the Levites and the poor ({{Deuteronomy 14:27-29|Deuteronomy 14:27–29}}; {{Deuteronomy 26:12|26:12}}; see {{Amos 4:4|Amos 4:4}} for contrast). The Levites then gave a tithe of what they received to the priests of the tabernacle ({{Numbers 18:26|Numbers 18:26}}). They used it for their support and to maintain the sanctuary. 

Some interpreters believe there were three tithes: 

- the first for the Levites, 

- the second consumed at the sanctuary, and 

- the third for the poor every third year. 

Others think there was one tithe, given at the sanctuary for two years, then locally every third year.
The penalty to buy back a tithed harvest was the same as the fine for someone who accidentally failed to give a tithe (see {{Leviticus 5:16|Leviticus 5:16}}).
Just like the crops from the fields, people also gave a tenth of the flocks and herds to God ({{Leviticus 27:29-34|Leviticus 27:29–34}}).
The book ends the way it began (see {{Leviticus 1:1|Leviticus 1:1}}). It clearly shows that its message came from God through Moses.

1:1: And He called to Moshe, and Adonoy spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting, saying:

And it was when Mosheh had completed to erect the tabernacle that Mosheh reasoned and judged in his heart, and said: To Mount Sinai, whose excellency is the excellence only of an hour and its holiness the holiness but of three days, I could not ascend till the time that the word was spoken to me; but the excellence of this the tabernacle of ordinance is an eternal excellency, and its holiness an everlasting holiness; therefore is it right that I should not enter within it until the time that I am spoken with from before the Lord. Then did the word of the Lord call unto Mosheh and the Word of the Lord spake with him from the tabernacle of ordinance saying:
1:2: Speak to Bnei Yisroel and say to them; [if] a man among you will bring an offering to [before] Adonoy; of animals, cattle or sheep you should bring your offering.

Speak with the sons of Israel, and say to them: If a man of you,-but not of the rebellious worshippers of idols,-bring an oblation before the Lord, (it must be) from the clean cattle, from the oxen or from the sheep; but not from the wild beasts may you offer your oblations.
1:3: If his offering is a burnt-offering of cattle he shall bring an unblemished male; to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting he shall bring it, that it be favorably accepted from him before Adonoy.
If his oblation be a burnt offering of oxen, he shall bring a male unblemished to the door of the tabernacle of ordinance, and offer him to be accepted for himself before the Lord.
1:4: He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt-offering and it will be favorably accepted from him to achieve his atonement.
And he shall lay his right hand with firmness upon the head of the sacrifice, that it may be acceptable from him to propitiate on his behalf.
1:5: He shall slaughter the calf before Adonoy and the sons of Aharon, the kohanim, will bring the blood and they will sprinkle the blood all around the altar, which is at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.

And the slayer shall kill the ox at the place of slaughter before the Lord, and the sons of Aharon the priest shall bring the blood in vessels, and sprinkle the blood which is in the basins round about the altar that is at the door of the tabernacle of ordinance.
1:6: He shall skin the burnt-offering and cut it into its pieces [limbs].
And he shall take away the skin from the sacrifice, and divide him according to his members.
1:7: The sons of Aharon the kohein shall place [ignite] a fire on the altar and they shall arrange logs on the fire.
And the sons of Aharon the priest shall put fire upon the altar, and lay wood in order upon the fire;
1:8: The sons of Aharon, the kohanim, shall arrange the pieces [limbs], the head and the fat on the logs which are on the fire that is on the altar.
and the priests the sons of Aharon shall lay the members in order and the heart and the covering of the fat upon the wood that is on the fire upon the altar.
1:9: He shall wash its innards and its legs in water; and the kohein shall burn it all on the altar [for the purpose of] a burnt-offering, a fire-offering [an offering] of pleasing fragrance to [which is accepted with favor before] Adonoy.
And he shall wash the inwards and his legs with water; and the priest shall offer the whole upon the altar of burnt offering an oblation to be accepted with grace before the Lord.
1:10: If his offering is from flocks of sheep—of lambs or of goats—for a burnt-offering, he shall bring an unblemished male.
And if his oblation be of the flock, whether of the lambs or of the young goats, he shall bring a male unblemished.
1:11: He shall slaughter it on the north side of the altar before Adonoy; and the sons of Aharon, the kohanim, will sprinkle its blood all around the altar.
And the slayer shall kill it at the foot of the altar on the north side, before the Lord, and the priests the sons of Aharon shall sprinkle the blood that is in the basins upon the altar round about.
1:12: He shall sever it into its pieces [limbs]—and its head, and [remove] its fats; and the kohein shall arrange them on the logs which are on the fire that is on the altar.
And he shall divide it by its members, its head and its body, and the priest shall set them in order on the wood which is upon the fire on the altar.
1:13: He shall wash the innards and feet in water and the kohein shall bring it all and burn it on the altar. It is a burnt-offering; a fire-offering [an offering] of pleasing fragrance to [which is accepted with favor before] Adonoy.
And the inwards and his legs he shall wash with water, and the priest shall offer the whole and burn it at the altar of burnt sacrifice; it is an offering to be received with grace before the Lord.
1:14: If his burnt-offering to [before] Adonoy is of fowl, he shall bring either turtledoves or the young pigeons [as] his offering.

And if his oblation before the Lord be of birds he shall bring his oblation from the turtle doves or the young Of pigeons; but of the turtle doves he shall bring the largest, and of the pigeons the young ones.
1:15: The kohein shall bring it near the altar and nip off its head [with his fingernail] and burn it on the altar; and its blood shall be squeezed out onto the wall of the altar.
And the priest shall offer it upon the altar, and shall wring off its head, and burn upon the altar, and press out its blood at the side of the altar.
1:16: He shall remove its crop [together] with its feathers [excrement] and throw it beside the altar, eastward, to the place of [where they throw] the ashes.
And he shall remove its gullet and the contents thereof, and throw it by the eastern side of the altar in the place where they burn the cinders.
1:17: He shall rip it apart by its wings, not completely dividing it. The kohein shall burn it on the altar, on the logs which are on the fire; it is a burnt-offering, a fire-offering [an offering] of pleasing fragrance to [which is accepted with favor before] Adonoy.

And he shall cut it between its wings, but not to sever the wings from it; and the priest shall burn it at the altar upon the wood which is on the fire: it is a sacrifice, an oblation to be received with favour before the Lord.
2:1: When a person brings a meal-offering to [before] Adonoy, his offering shall be of fine flour; he shall pour oil upon it and place frankincense upon it.
But when a man will offer the oblation of mincha before the Lord, his oblation shall be of flour, and he shall pour oil upon it, and put incense thereon,
2:2: He shall bring it to the sons of Aharon, the kohanim; from there, [a kohein] takes his fistful—from its flour and oil—with all its frankincense. The kohein shall burn its memorial portion on the altar, a fire-offering [an offering] of pleasing fragrance to [which is accepted with favor before] Adonoy.

and bring it to the priests the sons of Aharon; and he shall take from thence his hand full of the meal and of the best of the oil, with all the frankincense; and the priest shall burn the goodly memorial at the altar, an oblation to be accepted with grace before the Lord.
2:3: Whatever remains of the meal-offering belongs to Aharon and his sons; [it is] holy of holies of the fire-offerings [offerings] of Adonoy.
And what remaineth of the mincha shall be Aharon's and his sons, most holy among the oblations of the Lord.
2:4: And when you bring a meal-offering that has been baked in an oven, [it shall be unleavened] matzoh-loaves of fine flour mixed with oil, or [unleavened] matzoh wafers smeared with oil.
And when thou wilt offer the oblation of a mincha of that which is baked in the oven, it shall be cakes of flour, unleavened and mixed with oil, and wafers unleavened, which are anointed with oil.
2:5: If your offering is a pan-baked meal offering, it shall be of fine flour mixed with oil; it shall be [unleavened] matzoh.
And if thy oblation of a mincha be from the pan, it shall be of flour mingled with oil, unleavened shall it be.
2:6: Break it into pieces and pour oil on it; it is a meal-offering.
He shall break it in pieces, and pour oil thereupon. It is a mincha.
2:7: If your offering is a deep-pan [which appears as if it has been ploughed out] meal offering, you shall make it with fine flour and oil.
And if thy oblation be a mincha from the gridiron, it shall be made of flour broiled with oil.
2:8: You shall bring the meal-offering that will be made in any of the aforementioned ways to [before] Adonoy. He shall bring it to the kohein and he will present it to the altar.

And the mincha which hath been made with the flour and the oil thou shalt bring in before the Lord, and the man who bringeth it shall present it to the priest, and the priest shall take it to the altar.
2:9: The kohein shall separate from the meal-offering its memorial portion and burn it on the altar, a fire-offering [an offering] of pleasing fragrance to [which is accepted with favor before] Adonoy.
And the priest shall separate from the mincha a memorial of praise, and burn it at the altar, an oblation to be accepted with grace before the Lord.
2:10: Whatever remains of the meal-offering belongs to Aharon and his sons; [it is] holy of holies [most holy] of the fire-offering [offerings] of Adonoy.
And what remaineth of the mincha shall be for Aharon and his sons, it is most holy among the oblations of the Lord.
2:11: All meal-offerings that you bring to [before] Adonoy are not to be made leavened, because all sourdough and all honey you shall not burn from them a fire-offering to [an offering before] Adonoy.
But no mincha which thou offerest to the Lord shalt thou make with leaven; for neither leaven nor honey mayest thou offer as an oblation before the Lord.
2:12: You shall bring them as a first [fruit-]offering to [before] Adonoy but they shall not go up [be placed atop] the altar as a pleasing fragrance [to be accepted with favor].
